questions.a: Format drift, fuzzy label boundaries, and style misses. Knowledge gaps and missing tools are different problems.

questions.q: Outputs are correct but wrapped in "Sure, here is the JSON". Which pattern is that and what do you do?
questions.a: Format drift. Instruct "return only the object", show one bare example, then use structured output if a parser still breaks.

questions.q: Borderline tickets flip between billing and bug. What do you add before a pile of examples?
questions.a: One-sentence definitions of each label and two tickets that sit on the boundary with the agreed label. Then measure. More easy examples will not teach the line.

questions.q: Why should you fix format with a schema before you analyse label errors?
questions.a: A prose wrapper makes automatic scoring noisy, so you cannot see real boundary errors. Enforce shape first, then look at content tags.

questions.q: The model invents a SKU that is not in the prompt. Is that a few-shot problem?
questions.a: No. That is missing knowledge or a missing escape hatch. Retrieve the catalogue or allow `unknown`; do not add unrelated labelled tickets.

how-many-examples-to-use.explain:
## What it is

**How many examples** is an empirical stop rule, not a folklore number. A practical start is **three to five targeted cases** that cover the failures you already measured. You add another only if the test set still moves. You stop when it does not. You also stop if the extra tokens cost more than the quality they buy.

There is no universal k. Some format tasks need one shot. Some 12-way taxonomies need one example per rare class and still do better with a schema than with 24 shots. Returns diminish; context is finite; recency and imbalance get worse as the block grows.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is how few-shot dies of success: someone adds an example per incident until the prefix is 3,000 tokens and last month's eval has silently regressed. A stop rule — "we add a shot only when this slice's score rises and nothing else falls" — keeps the prefix honest.

Interviewers sometimes ask "how many examples do you use?" The wrong answer is a single number. The right answer is the start-of-three-to-five, the stop-when-the-set-stalls rule, and the reminder that one great borderline shot beats ten easy ones.

## How it works + one small example

Procedure:

1. Zero-shot baseline on the fixed set. Record pass rate, tokens, latency.
2. Add 3 shots: canonical, borderline, abstain. Re-run.
3. If a tagged slice is still weak, add **one** shot for that slice. Re-run the **whole** set, not just the slice.
4. Stop when the whole-set score is flat (or a regression appears). Revert the last add.
5. If format is still dirty after one shot, switch to structured output rather than shooting to k=15.

```
k=0  acc=0.78  in_tok=420
k=3  acc=0.86  in_tok=910
k=4  acc=0.86  in_tok=1100   # stop; last shot did nothing
```

For many-class problems, prefer **one shot per rare class** plus a couple of majority-class shots, not N per class. Coverage beats multiplication.

## Failure modes

1. **Incident-driven growth.** Each production miss becomes a new example. The prefix becomes a diary and yesterday's fix is tomorrow's recency bias.

2. **Counting instead of targeting.** Eight easy majority-class shots look like "we few-shot" and do not touch the slice you fail.

3. **Ignoring the bill.** A 4-point gain that doubles input tokens on a hot path may be worse than a clearer zero-shot or a smaller model. Measure cost with quality.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I start with three to five targeted examples — a clear case, a borderline, an abstain — and I stop when the test set stops improving. I add at most one shot per remaining weak slice and I re-run the whole set so I see regressions. If format is still dirty, I use a schema, not k=15.
## Worked scenario

Baseline k=0 is 0.78. k=3 (canonical, borderline, abstain) is 0.86. k=4 is 0.86 with more tokens. You ship k=3. A month of incidents wants to grow the block. You add incidents to the **eval set** instead, and only promote a shot when the whole-set score rises. The prefix stays a design, not a diary.

For a 12-label taxonomy you add one shot per rare miss, not twelve shots by reflex. Coverage of the line you fail beats multiplication of the line you already pass.

If format is still dirty at k=1, you do not walk to k=15. You turn on a schema. Count is not a format strategy.

## Interview trap

The trap is a folklore number ('we always use seven'). The stop rule is: start at three to five targeted shots, add one only if a slice still fails, re-run the whole set, revert a no-op. Incident-driven growth turns the prefix into a diary and wrecks recency. If format is still dirty at k=1, a schema beats k=15.
keyPoints: Start with three to five targeted cases, not a folklore dozen.
Add one shot at a time and re-run the whole eval set.
Stop when the set is flat or a regression appears; revert the last add.
One borderline shot beats ten easy majority-class shots.
For many classes, cover rare labels; do not multiply easy ones.
If format still fails after one shot, enforce a schema instead of growing k.

questions.q: What stop rule do you use for the number of few-shot examples?
questions.a: Start with three to five targeted cases. Add one shot only if a weak slice still fails, re-run the whole set, and stop when scores flatten or regress. Revert the last no-op add.

questions.q: k=3 is 86% and k=4 is 86% with more tokens. What do you ship?
questions.a: k=3. The fourth shot did not buy quality. Keep the cheaper prefix and spend effort on the remaining tagged misses another way.

questions.q: A 12-label taxonomy has two rare classes you always miss. Do you add 12 examples?
questions.a: No. Add one carefully written shot for each rare class (and keep the set balanced) rather than one per class by default. Measure; a definition change may beat more shots.

questions.q: Why re-run the whole set after adding a shot for one slice?
questions.a: A new example can recency-bias other labels or teach a format that breaks a different case. Slice-only testing hides regressions.

questions.q: Production keeps growing the example block by one ticket per incident. What do you change?
questions.a: Freeze the block, move new incidents into the eval set, and only promote a shot when the whole-set metric rises. The prefix is not an incident log.

dynamic-few-shot-from-a-store.explain:
## What it is

**Dynamic few-shot** means you do not hard-code a static example block. You keep a **store** of labelled inputs — a table, a vector index, even a folder of JSON — and at request time you **retrieve** the examples most similar to this input, then splice them into the prompt. The instruction stays static; the demonstrations follow the query.

This is few-shot plus retrieval. It helps when the task is the same but the input space is wide: many product lines, many languages, many ticket subtypes. It is unnecessary when three static shots already clear the bar.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a static block is easier to cache, review, and replay. A dynamic block can lift quality on the long tail — the Finnish ticket, the enterprise SKU, the legal clause type you see twice a month — without stuffing fifty shots into every call. The trade is operational: you now have an index to keep clean, a retrieval bug class, and traces that must record which example ids were chosen or you cannot reproduce a failure.

Interviewers use this to see if you know that "RAG" is not only documents. Retrieving labelled demonstrations is the same idea applied to behaviour. They also want to hear the cache warning: retrieved shots belong in the suffix (or a per-request section), not in the byte-stable prefix.

## How it works + one small example

A minimal design:

1. Store `{id, input, output, label, tags}` you would be willing to show the model.
2. Embed `input` (or a cheap lexical search) and, at request time, take top-k similar to the live ticket.
3. Enforce a **label quota** so k=4 cannot return four `billing` neighbours.
4. Render them in the same delimiters as static shots, after the rules, before the live ticket.
5. Log `example_ids` and scores on the trace.

```
# request for a sarcastic billing ticket
retrieved: ex_88 (billing, sarcasm), ex_12 (billing, refund), ex_41 (other, empty)
```

Start with k=3. Use the same stop rule as static few-shot. If lexical search finds the right rare class, you do not need embeddings on day one.

## Failure modes

1. **No quota.** Nearest neighbours are all the majority class. You re-introduced imbalance, only dynamically.

2. **Stale or poisoned store.** A mislabelled ticket, or a ticket that contains an injection, is now a teacher for similar live tickets. Review joins; treat store rows as production data.

3. **Unlogged retrieval.** A user reports a bad label and you cannot see which shots were in the prompt. The bug is unreproducible. Log ids.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

When the input space is wide I retrieve a few similar labelled examples at request time instead of hard-coding a giant static block. I quota labels, I log the ids, and I keep those shots out of the cacheable prefix. If three static examples already pass the eval, I do not build a store.
## Worked scenario

A global support queue has Finnish and Japanese tickets that static English shots never cover. You store labelled tickets (redacted) and retrieve k=3 neighbours per request, with a label quota. You log `example_ids`. A bad Finnish label is now replayable. Those shots sit in the suffix so the rule prefix still caches.

The store gets a poisoned row: a ticket that says "ignore previous instructions". You treat store rows as untrusted, fence them, and review joins. Nearest neighbour is not a trust boundary.

If three static shots already clear the bar, you do not build this. Dynamic few-shot is for a wide input space, not for prestige.
keyPoints: Dynamic few-shot retrieves similar labelled examples per request.
Use it when the input space is wide and a static block cannot cover the tail.
Enforce a label quota so neighbours are not all one class.
Log example ids on every trace or you cannot replay a failure.
Put retrieved shots in the suffix so the rule prefix still caches.
The store is production data: review labels and watch for poisoned rows.

questions.q: What is dynamic few-shot, in one sentence?
questions.a: At request time you retrieve a few similar labelled examples from a store and splice them into the prompt, instead of always sending the same hard-coded shots.

questions.q: Why can nearest-neighbour examples make a classifier worse?
questions.a: If the neighbourhood is mostly one class, you dynamically unbalance the prompt. Quota labels (and mix a hard negative) before you raise k.

questions.q: Where do retrieved examples sit in a caching-friendly prompt?
questions.a: After the stable rules prefix, in the per-request suffix, so the cache key does not include this query's neighbours.

questions.q: What must you log for a dynamic few-shot call?
questions.a: The example ids (and ideally similarity scores) plus prompt version and model, so a bad output can be replayed with the same demonstrations.

questions.q: A retrieved example contains "ignore previous instructions". What is the risk?
questions.a: Indirect injection via your own store. Review and fence store rows like any untrusted text; do not treat labelled data as automatically safe.

label-balance-and-recency-bias.explain:
## What it is

**Label balance** means the examples you show do not massively over-represent one class relative to the decision you want. **Recency bias** means models often overweight the last thing they read, so a prompt that ends with three `urgent` tickets will tilt the next ambiguous ticket toward `urgent`. They interact: an imbalanced set that also clusters the majority class at the end is a doubly loaded die.

This is the same bias story as in ordinary datasets, except the "dataset" is twelve lines in a prompt and you can wreck it in a one-line edit.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, people collect examples from yesterday's failures. Yesterday was a billing outage, so the block becomes billing, billing, billing. Today's bug tickets then look like billing. The eval average may even rise if billing is common; the rare class dies.

Interviewers will draw five examples, four of them `spam`, last one `spam`, and ask what happens. You should say: over-prediction of spam, especially on ambiguous inputs; fix by mixing classes and not ending on a run of one label. Bonus points if you mention you would not shuffle live because of caching.

## How it works + one small example

For a static block:

- Aim for **roughly even shots** across labels you care about, plus extra only for a rare class you systematically miss.
- **Interleave** labels rather than grouping them.
- Put a **hard mixed case last** if you put anything last on purpose — or put the abstain example last so the escape hatch is fresh — and measure both.
- For dynamic retrieval, apply a **quota**: max two of the same label in k=5, fill remaining slots from the next neighbours.

```
# bad tail
... bug, bug, billing, billing, billing

# better tail
... billing, bug, how-to, other, billing-sarcasm
```

If your live prior is 90% `how-to`, you still should not show 90% `how-to` shots if the errors you care about are the 10%. Balance the **teaching set** for the decision boundary, not for traffic share. Traffic share belongs in evaluation weighting, not necessarily in the prompt.

## Failure modes

1. **Failure-driven collection.** You only add misses, and misses this month are one class. The block drifts. Rebalance on a schedule.

2. **Ending on the majority.** Even a balanced count can bias if the last three are the same. Look at the tail, not only the histogram.

3. **Fighting recency with live shuffle.** You trade one bias for unreproducible, uncacheable prompts. Fix the static order.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I treat the example block like a tiny dataset: mix classes, do not cluster one label at the end, and I do not let last week's incidents rewrite the mix. Recency bias is real, so I inspect the tail and I test order; I do not shuffle a live prefix.
## Worked scenario

After a billing outage the example block is five billing tickets, last three clustered. Bug tickets look like billing for a week. You rebalance on a calendar, not from last night's incidents, and you inspect the tail. A hard mixed case sits last because you measured that order; you did not shuffle.

Traffic is 90% how-to. You still do not show 90% how-to shots, because the errors you care about are the 10%. Traffic weights the eval; the teaching set covers the boundary.

A teammate shuffles to "cancel recency" and cache dies. You restore a balanced static order. Recency is a tail problem, not a reason to randomise production.

## Interview trap

They will draw four spam shots with a spam tail and ask what happens. Say over-prediction on ambiguous inputs, then interleave and inspect the tail. Do not shuffle a live prefix to 'fix recency' — that kills cache and replay. Balance the teaching set for the boundary you miss, not for the 90% traffic prior.
keyPoints: Imbalanced shots teach the majority class as the default.
Recency bias overweight the last examples, especially on ambiguous inputs.
Interleave labels; inspect the tail, not only the class counts.
Balance the teaching set for the boundary you care about, not raw traffic share.
Quota labels when you retrieve examples dynamically.
Do not shuffle a production prefix just to fight recency.

questions.q: What is recency bias in a few-shot prompt?
questions.a: The model leans toward patterns in the last examples it read, so a tail of one label can pull ambiguous cases toward that label.

questions.q: Four of five examples are spam and the last three are spam. What do you expect?
questions.a: Over-prediction of spam, worse on borderline inputs. Rebalance, interleave, and stop ending on a spam run.

questions.q: Why might you not mirror the 90% how-to traffic prior in the example block?
questions.a: The teaching set should cover the boundary you miss, often the rare classes. Traffic share can weight the eval; it does not have to dominate the shots.

questions.q: Dynamic retrieval returns five billing neighbours. What control did you forget?
questions.a: A label quota (and maybe a hard negative slot) so k cannot collapse to one class.

questions.q: A teammate shuffles examples each call to "cancel recency". What do you change?
questions.a: Restore a balanced static order so the prefix caches and traces replay. Recency is handled by interleaving and by testing one or two fixed orders.

cost-of-few-shot-vs-a-clearer-instructio.explain:
## What it is

Every example you keep is a **recurring token cost**: input tokens on every call, extra latency, and a larger prefix that may or may not cache. A **clearer instruction** — a sharper label definition, a better output spec, one sentence about sarcasm — is paid once in the template and is usually shorter. The discipline is to **measure both** on the same test set before you keep the shots.

This is not anti-example. It is anti-unmeasured example. If three shots add 4 points and 80 tokens, keep them. If they add 0 points and 80 tokens, delete them. If a 20-token rewrite of the zero-shot matches the shots, ship the rewrite.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this shows up on the bill two months later. A "temporary" five-example block on a hot classifier is now most of the input spend. Nobody remembered to re-run the zero-shot. The professional move is a table: variant, accuracy, input tokens, p95 latency, cost per 1k requests. Pick the cheapest that clears the quality bar.

Interviewers ask how you would cut cost without losing quality. "Delete the examples and hope" is wrong. "Compare the few-shot against a rewritten zero-shot on the same set, then cache the prefix if shots stay" is the Level 3 answer.

## How it works + one small example

Run three variants on the same 50 cases, same model, same temperature:

```
A  zero-shot original          acc 0.80  in 180 tok
B  zero-shot + 4-line defs     acc 0.87  in 240 tok
C  original + 4 examples       acc 0.87  in 900 tok
```

Ship B. Keep C in the notebook as a reference. If B had stayed at 0.80 and C hit 0.90, ship C and put the shots in the cacheable prefix.

Also compare **structured output** as a fourth variant when the only gap is format. A schema can beat both A and C on parse rate at almost no extra input tokens.

Write the comparison down next to the prompt version. Future you will try to add the examples back "just in case".

## Failure modes

1. **Comparing on vibes.** You read two playground outputs and keep the longer prompt. That is not a measurement.

2. **Ignoring cache.** Four static examples in a stable prefix may be almost free after the first call. Four dynamic examples in the suffix are full price every time. Cost depends on layout.

3. **Optimising cost before a quality bar exists.** You will delete the shots that hold a rare class and celebrate a cheaper, worse product. Define the bar first.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I do not keep examples out of habit. I run the few-shot against a rewritten zero-shot on the same set and I look at accuracy, tokens, and p95 together. I ship the cheapest variant that clears the bar, and I put any surviving static shots in the cacheable prefix.
## Worked scenario

You run three variants on 50 cases. Original zero-shot 0.80 / 180 tok. Sharper four-line definitions 0.87 / 240 tok. Original plus four examples 0.87 / 900 tok. You ship the definitions. The examples stay in the notebook. Two months later the prefix would have been most of the bill if you had kept them.

Those four examples, had they sat in a cached prefix, would have been cheaper than they looked in a cold playground. You still would have shipped the 240-token version, because it matched quality without depending on cache TTL.

Define the bar before you delete shots. A cheaper prompt that dropped the rare class is not a win. Cost is a tie-break after the bar.

## Interview trap

Keep a table: rewritten zero-shot vs few-shot on the same set, with tokens and p95. If definitions match shots at a third of the tokens, ship the definitions. Static shots in a cached prefix are cheaper than they look in a cold playground; dynamic shots in the suffix are not. Never cut shots until you know which slice they held.
keyPoints: Examples are a recurring token cost; a clearer instruction is usually cheaper.
Compare few-shot vs rewritten zero-shot on the same set before keeping shots.
Pick the cheapest variant that clears a pre-set quality bar.
Static shots in a cached prefix are cheaper than dynamic shots in the suffix.
A schema can beat both variants when the only miss is format.
Do not cut examples until you know which slice they were holding up.

questions.q: What do you measure before you keep a few-shot block?
questions.a: Quality on a fixed set, input tokens, latency, and cost per request, compared to a rewritten zero-shot (and to structured output if format is the issue).

questions.q: Variant B (sharper defs) matches variant C (four examples) at a third of the tokens. What do you ship?
questions.a: B. The examples are not earning their keep. Keep C in the notebook and re-check if a new slice appears.

questions.q: Four static examples look expensive in the playground but cheap in production. Why might that be?
questions.a: They sit in a byte-stable prefix and prompt caching discounts later calls. Dynamic or shuffled examples would not get that discount.

questions.q: Why define a quality bar before you delete examples to save money?
questions.a: Otherwise you will ship a cheaper prompt that dropped a rare class you care about. Cost is a tie-break after the bar, not a goal on its own.

questions.q: Format errors dominate. Should you add examples or change the API?
questions.a: Try one exact-shape example, then prefer a structured-output / schema API. Extra shots are a slow, leaky way to do decoding.

choosing-zero-shot-few-shot-or-fine-tune.explain:
## What it is

**Choosing zero-shot, few-shot, or fine-tune** is a cost-and-ops decision on top of a quality bar. You pick the **cheapest method that hits the measured bar**, in that order of operational weight: zero-shot (instruction + schema), then few-shot (a few demonstrations), then fine-tune (weights). You do not skip to the heavy tool because it sounds advanced.

"Cheapest" includes human time. A one-day fine-tune that you must re-run monthly can lose to a prompt you change in an hour. "Hits the bar" is measured on a held-out set, not on the example you just added.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the decision interviewers actually want. They will describe a task and wait to see if you jump to training. The senior path is a ladder: write the contract, measure, add targeted shots if the miss is format/boundary/style, enforce schema if the miss is parse, retrieve if the miss is facts, tune only if volume, latency, or stubborn style still fail the bar with enough labels to do it honestly.

On the job the same ladder keeps you from owning a graveyard of adapters that exist because someone skipped structured output.

## How it works + one small example

Use this ladder on a real task (illustrative thresholds, not laws):

1. **Zero-shot + output spec.** If pass rate ≥ bar, stop.
2. **Schema / structured output** if failures are parse errors.
3. **3–5 targeted shots** if failures are boundaries or style. Re-measure tokens.
4. **Retrieval or a tool** if failures are missing facts.
5. **Fine-tune** if you have enough labels, a hold-out, and a reason: huge volume, need a smaller model, or a style that prompting cannot hold after a fair try.

Example: invoice-field extraction. Zero-shot + JSON schema hits 96% valid objects and 91% field F1. Bar was 90% F1 and 99% valid. You do not few-shot and you do not tune; you add a validate/retry for the 4% invalids. Another example: brand-voice emails at 8 million/day. Prompting hits the voice bar but the prefix is huge. Now a tuned small model is in play.

Write the chosen rung on the prompt's README: `method=few-shot@4, bar=0.90, measured=0.92, next=stop`.

## Failure modes

1. **Skipping rungs.** Fine-tune first because a vendor dashboard made it one click. You now own weights for a problem a schema would have solved.

2. **No bar.** Without a number, every method is "not quite good enough" and you keep adding machinery.

3. **Mixing facts into the method choice.** A catalogue problem is a retrieval problem at every rung. Tuning or few-shoting SKUs is the wrong axis.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I pick the cheapest method that hits a measured quality bar: zero-shot and a schema first, targeted few-shot next, retrieval for facts, fine-tune last when I have labels and a volume or style reason. I write the bar down so the choice is a table, not a taste.
## Worked scenario

Invoice extraction: zero-shot plus schema hits 96% valid and 91% field F1. Bar was 90% F1 and 99% valid. You add validate/retry for the 4% invalids. You do not few-shot and you do not tune. Brand-voice mail at 8 million a day is the opposite: prompting hits voice but the prefix is huge, so a tuned small model enters the conversation with a hold-out.

Write `method=schema+retry, bar=0.90/0.99, measured=0.91/0.997` on the README. A teammate who wants to fine-tune because few-shot "feels junior" is arguing prestige. The table wins.

Facts that change (catalogues) are retrieval at every rung. If the miss is knowledge, climbing toward weights is the wrong axis.
keyPoints: Climb the ladder: zero-shot, schema, few-shot, retrieval, then fine-tune.
Ship the cheapest method that clears a written quality bar.
Cheapest includes human and ops time, not only token price.
Do not fine-tune to fix JSON or to store a changing catalogue.
Write the chosen rung, the bar, and the measured score next to the prompt.
No bar means you will keep adding machinery forever.

questions.q: In what order do you try zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuning?
questions.a: Zero-shot (plus a schema if needed), then targeted few-shot, then fine-tune if labels, a hold-out, and a cost or style reason remain. Retrieve at any point if the miss is facts.

questions.q: Invoice extraction already meets the F1 bar with a schema but 4% of objects fail to parse. Fine-tune?
questions.a: No. Add validate/retry or constrained decoding for the invalids. Fine-tuning is the wrong tool for residual parse errors.

questions.q: A teammate wants to fine-tune because few-shot "feels more junior". What do you say?
questions.a: Method is chosen by a measured bar and cost, not by prestige. If few-shot clears the bar cheaper, it is the senior choice.

questions.q: What belongs on the prompt README after you choose a method?
questions.a: The rung you picked, the quality bar, the measured score, token/latency notes, and what would make you climb to the next rung.

questions.q: 8 million brand-voice emails a day, prompt hits quality but the prefix is huge. Which way do you look?
questions.a: Now fine-tuning a smaller model (or caching a static prefix, or both) is in play, because volume makes prefix tokens the bill. Still keep a hold-out eval.

when-to-prompt-for-reasoning.explain:
## What it is

**Reasoning-oriented prompting** means you ask the model to spend tokens on intermediate work before it commits to an answer: a short plan, a chain of calculations, a comparison against constraints. Those tokens act as working memory because each generated token conditions the next. You use this when the task has **dependent steps** — logic, planning, mathematics, coding, multi-constraint decisions — not when the task is a single lookup.

This includes classic "think step by step" on a chat model and the more modern pattern of sending work to a **reasoning model** with an effort budget. The point is the same: do not force the answer in sentence one if the answer depends on work that has not happened yet.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a planner that writes a migration order, a debugger that traces a stack, or a pricing engine that applies three discounts in sequence will silently fail if you demand the final JSON first. Visible or hidden intermediate work is how you buy accuracy. It also costs latency and output tokens, so you turn it on where a test set says it pays.

Interviewers will ask when you use chain-of-thought. The answer is: multi-step, constraint-heavy, math, code, planning — and I measure. They may also ask you to put the answer after the work. Putting "Answer:" first is a common self-inflicted bug.

## How it works + one small example

Ask for work **before** the commit, and separate them so a parser can ignore the work.

```
Work through the discounts in order (member 10%, then coupon $5, then tax 8%).
Show the running total after each step.
Then return only {"total_cents": int} after the marker END.
```

For coding: "List the failing invariant, name the function, then patch." For planning: "List constraints you will honour, then the ordered steps." For classification with a hard boundary: "Quote the sentence that decides the label, then the label." The quote is the reasoning; the label is the answer.

If you use a reasoning model, you often do **not** add "think step by step"; you state the goal, the constraints, and the output schema, and you set the effort parameter. Check the current provider docs.

## Failure modes

1. **Answer first, story later.** "Give the total, then explain." The explanation will rationalise a guess. Reverse it.

2. **Reasoning on a single-step task.** You pay for a paragraph that restates the email and then says `billing`. Accuracy does not move; the bill does.

3. **Treating the trace as an audit log.** Fluent steps can be a plausible story, not the true computation. Score the final answer against gold; do not trust the essay.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I prompt for reasoning when the task has dependent steps — math, code, planning, hard constraints — and I make the model work before it answers. I separate the scratch work from the parsed result, and I only keep the extra tokens if a test set shows a gain.
## Worked scenario

A pricing function stacks member 10%, coupon $5, then tax. Asking for the total first yields confident wrong numbers. You require a running total after each step, then `{"total_cents": int}` after `END`. Accuracy jumps. You parse the field, not the essay. You do not store the essay as the official reason for a credit.

On a tagger, the same "think step by step" doubles output tokens and does nothing. You keep reasoning where the eval shows dependent steps — math, code, planning, multi-constraint — and you turn it off elsewhere.

If you use a reasoning model, you state goal and constraints and set effort; you do not paste a chat-model CoT script. Check current provider notes; they change.
keyPoints: Ask for intermediate work when the task has dependent steps.
Generated tokens are working memory; the answer must come after the work.
Use it for math, code, planning, and multi-constraint decisions.
Separate scratch work from the parsed final field.
Reasoning models often need a goal and an effort budget, not "think step by step".
Fluent traces are not a faithful audit; score the final answer.

questions.q: Why does asking for reasoning before the answer help on multi-step problems?
questions.a: Each generated token conditions the next, so intermediate steps give the model workspace. If the answer is emitted first, later text can only rationalise it.

questions.q: A prompt says "Give the answer, then explain." Math accuracy is poor. What changes?
questions.a: Reverse the order: compute first, then emit the final field after a marker. The current order commits before the work exists.

questions.q: Name three task types that usually deserve reasoning tokens.
questions.a: Multi-step math or pricing, code debugging or implementation with constraints, and planning or comparison against several rules. Single-step extract and rewrite usually do not.

questions.q: How would you structure a discount-stack prompt?
questions.a: Instruct the model to apply discounts in a stated order, show a running total after each, then output only a typed total field. Parse the field, not the essay.

questions.q: A stakeholder wants to store chain-of-thought as the official reason for a credit decision. What do you say?
questions.a: Visible reasoning can be unfaithful. Use it to improve accuracy, not as a compliance explanation. If you need an audit, write a separate, checked justification path.

when-reasoning-is-unnecessary.explain:
## What it is

**Reasoning is unnecessary** when the task is single-step: extraction, classification with clear rules, rewriting, formatting, lookup from provided text. Extra "think step by step" then adds output tokens, latency, and sometimes **overthinking** — the model talks itself out of a correct first instinct or invents a constraint you did not write.

Reasoning-trained models already spend hidden tokens. Stacking a verbal chain-of-thought on top often duplicates cost. The decision is empirical: same test set, with and without, compare accuracy, p95, and tokens.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is a common silent bill. A high-volume tagger inherited "let's think step by step" from a blog. Cost doubled. Accuracy did not move. Removing one sentence is a better optimisation than a week of caching work.

Interviewers use this to see if you can turn techniques off. Enthusiasm for chain-of-thought without a stop condition looks junior. "I A/B it and I route only hard cases" looks like production sense.

## How it works + one small example

Signs you can skip reasoning:

- One document, one field, one label.
- The instruction fully determines the output (`Title Case the heading`).
- You already enforce a schema and the errors are not logical.
- Latency budget is tight and the eval does not improve with a scratchpad.

Signs you should keep it: multi-hop questions, overlapping constraints, arithmetic, planning with irreversible tools.

Hybrid: a cheap router (rules or a small model) sends easy tickets to a direct prompt and hard ones to a reasoning variant. Measure both arms.

```
# A/B on 50 cases
direct:     acc 0.93  p95 400ms  out_tok 40
reason:     acc 0.93  p95 2.1s   out_tok 280
# delete the reasoning instruction
```

If a reasoning model is in use, prefer lowering the effort setting rather than adding more verbal steps.

## Failure modes

1. **Habit.** Every prompt in the repo starts with step-by-step because the first one did. Audit and delete.

2. **Overthinking regressions.** A simple extractor starts omitting fields after you ask it to "reason about completeness". The extra narrative crowded out the schema. Drop the narrative; keep the schema.

3. **Hidden + visible reasoning stacked.** You pay twice and you still parse the wrong channel. Read the provider's current guidance.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I do not add reasoning to extraction, clean classification, or rewrites unless a test set says I must. Extra steps cost tokens and can overthink a simple task. I A/B with and without, and I route only the hard slice to a reasoning prompt or a higher effort setting.
## Worked scenario

A high-volume tagger inherited "let's think step by step" from a blog. You A/B 50 cases: same 0.93 accuracy, p95 400ms vs 2.1s. You delete the sentence and optionally route only low-confidence items to a reasoning variant. The bill drops more than a week of caching work would have.

An extractor you asked to "reason about completeness" starts omitting fields. The narrative crowded the schema. You drop the steps, keep the schema, and score missing fields separately.

Habit is the enemy. Audit the repo for stacked CoT on reasoning models and for CoT on single-step paths. Turning a technique off is a senior move.

## Interview trap

Enthusiasm without a stop condition looks junior. A/B with and without on the same set. Extraction, clean classification, and rewrites usually do not pay. Overthinking can drop fields. Reasoning models already think; stacked verbal CoT often bills twice. Route only the hard slice. Turning the technique off is the senior move.
keyPoints: Skip extra reasoning on single-step extract, classify, and rewrite work.
Measure with and without on the same set; do not keep it as habit.
Overthinking can drop fields or invent constraints you did not write.
Reasoning models already think; stacked verbal CoT often wastes tokens.
Route easy cases to a direct prompt and hard cases to a reasoning variant.
Lower effort before you add more "think step by step" text.

questions.q: Name two task types where chain-of-thought is usually wasted.
questions.a: Plain extraction or formatting, and simple classification with clear rules. They are single-step, so extra reasoning mainly raises cost and latency.

questions.q: A high-volume tagger added "think step by step" and cost doubled with no accuracy gain. What do you do?
questions.a: Confirm on the test set, remove the instruction, and optionally route only low-confidence items to a reasoning variant.

questions.q: An extractor starts omitting fields after you ask it to reason about completeness. Likely cause?
questions.a: Overthinking: the narrative crowded out the schema. Drop the forced steps, keep the schema, and score missing fields separately.

questions.q: How do you decide whether reasoning is unnecessary for a new task?
questions.a: Run the same eval with and without (or at two effort levels). If accuracy is flat and latency or tokens rose, it is unnecessary.

questions.q: You use a reasoning model and also wrote a long chain-of-thought script. What should you try?
questions.a: Delete the scripted steps, state goal and constraints, and tune the effort parameter. Check the provider's current prompting notes.

decomposing-complex-tasks.explain:
## What it is

**Decomposition** splits a large job into smaller prompts or stages, each simple enough to do reliably and to test alone. Instead of "read the contract, find risks, rank them, and draft an email", you extract clauses, assess each clause, rank the assessments, then draft from a structured list. Each hop has its own contract.

Decomposition is not the same as chain-of-thought inside one call. CoT is extra tokens in one generation. Decomposition is extra **calls** (or extra validated fields) with code in between. You use it when one prompt is mixing skills that fail independently.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a single mega-prompt that extracts, judges, and writes will fail in ways you cannot localise. Was the extraction wrong or the judgement? You cannot tell from a polished memo. Split, and you can unit-test the extractor with a schema, run a cheaper model on the easy hop, and stop a bad extract from reaching the customer.

Interviewers love a decomposition sketch. They also love hearing when you would **not** split (see the later note): every hop can drop a field. The senior answer names both.

## How it works + one small example

Common patterns:

- **Chain:** output of A is input to B, with a schema check between.
- **Route:** classify first, then dispatch to a specialised prompt.
- **Fan-out:** map a list of clauses in parallel, then merge.
- **Plan-then-execute:** write a plan object, approve it (code or human), then execute steps.

Contract review sketch:

```
1) extract_clauses -> {id, text}[]     # schema, cheap model
2) assess_each     -> {id, risk, why}  # one clause per call
3) rank            -> top 5 ids        # deterministic sort + model tie-break
4) draft_email     -> prose from top 5 # no new facts allowed
```

Validate at each edge. If step 1 returns an empty list, do not invent risks in step 2.

## Failure modes

1. **Too many hops.** A simple label job becomes four calls. Latency and cost explode and a field is dropped on hop 2. Split only when a single prompt shows mixed skills failing.

2. **No validation between hops.** Errors propagate; the last hop writes a confident email from garbage.

3. **Hidden coupling.** Step 4 still re-reads the raw contract and ignores the structured list, so you paid for unused hops.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I split a task when one prompt is mixing skills that fail independently: extract, then judge, then write, with a schema between hops. I can test and cheapen each stage. I do not split a simple extract-and-label job just to look architectural.
## Worked scenario

A contract memo prompt extracts, judges, and writes in one call. Reports look polished and are locally wrong. You split: extract `{id,text}[]` with a schema, assess each clause, rank in code, draft only from the top five. The writer is forbidden from re-reading the PDF. Each hop has a test. A cheap model does hop 1.

You do not split a simple label job into four calls. That is ceremony. The heuristic: if you cannot name a check hop N adds, delete it. If the last hop ignores the structured list, you paid for unused architecture.

Validation between hops is what makes this better than a longer CoT. Without it, errors just travel farther.

## Interview trap

They will push you to split everything. Split when one prompt mixes skills that fail independently, with a schema between hops. Do not split a label job into four calls. If hop N only restates hop N-1, delete it. If the writer re-reads the PDF, you paid for unused architecture. Validation between hops is the whole point.
keyPoints: Decomposition is multiple validated stages, not just longer chain-of-thought.
Patterns: chain, route, fan-out, plan-then-execute.
Validate with a schema between hops so errors do not propagate.
Use a cheaper model on easy stages when the eval allows it.
Split only when a single prompt mixes skills that fail separately.
If the last hop re-reads the raw source, you wasted the earlier hops.

questions.q: List benefits and costs of decomposing a task into a prompt chain.
questions.a: Benefits: focused prompts, per-step tests, validation, cheaper models on easy hops. Costs: extra latency and tokens, and error propagation if you do not validate between stages.

questions.q: A single prompt extracts facts, judges them, and writes a report inconsistently. How do you restructure it?
questions.a: Split into extract (schema), judge (per fact, with criteria), then write from the validated judgements only. Evaluate each stage and block the writer from inventing new facts.

questions.q: Step 4 of your chain ignores the structured list and rereads the PDF. What is wrong?
questions.a: The last prompt is coupled to the raw source, so earlier hops are unused cost. Constrain the writer to the structured list and drop the PDF from that call.

questions.q: Name the four common decomposition patterns.
questions.a: Prompt chaining, routing after a classifier, parallel fan-out then merge, and plan-then-execute.

questions.q: When would you refuse to decompose?
questions.a: When the task is simple extract-and-label and a single schema-backed call already meets the bar. Extra hops can drop fields and add latency for no gain.

prompting-reasoning-models.explain:
## What it is

**Reasoning models** are trained to spend extra tokens on internal work before they answer. Providers expose that as an effort, budget, or "thinking" setting. Prompting them is different from prompting a classic chat model: you state the **goal, constraints, and output shape** clearly, and you usually **do not** script "think step by step" or pile on few-shot traces. They already allocate scratch space.

Hidden reasoning tokens are typically billed as output and count toward max-output limits. If you set a small `max_tokens`, you can get a long wait and an empty or truncated answer.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, teams copy their old CoT prompts onto a reasoning model, double the bill, and sometimes **hurt** quality by over-constraining the approach. The new skill is: simpler prompts, explicit constraints, enough output budget, and an effort knob you treat like a cost control.

Interviewers will ask how prompting changes. Say: goal and constraints, skip redundant step-by-step, test whether examples help (they can hurt), set effort against latency, watch reasoning-token usage. Mention that provider guidance changes and you read it.

## How it works + one small example

A good reasoning-model prompt is short:

```
Goal: choose a warehouse allocation that meets demand and capacity.
Constraints: do not exceed capacity[]; prefer lower shipping_cost.
Data: <demand>…</demand> <capacity>…</capacity>
Output: {"alloc": {warehouse: units}, "total_cost": number}
If infeasible, {"alloc": null, "reason": "infeasible"}.
```

You do not list eight steps. You do set effort=high for a hard instance and effort=low for a tiny one. You set max output high enough that the answer still fits after internal tokens. You log both reasoning-token and answer-token counts.

Few-shot: try zero first. A worked example can pin the model to a worse algorithm. If you use examples, show the **final object**, not a fake internal monologue.

## Failure modes

1. **Truncation by reasoning tokens.** Empty answer, long latency. Raise max output or lower effort; do not retry blindly.

2. **Micromanaged steps.** You force a method the model would have beaten. Delete the script; keep constraints.

3. **Using a reasoning model on a tagger.** You bought a race car for a driveway. Route simple work to a standard model.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

For reasoning models I write a short goal, hard constraints, and a schema. I skip "think step by step", I test examples before keeping them, and I budget output tokens so hidden thinking cannot eat the answer. I turn effort up only when the eval pays for it.
## Worked scenario

A warehouse allocation lands on a reasoning model with an eight-step script copied from a chat prompt. Latency is ugly and quality is worse than a short goal+constraints+schema prompt. You delete the script, set effort high only on infeasible-looking instances, and raise max output so hidden tokens cannot eat the answer. Empty truncated answers disappear.

You try one few-shot trace; it pins a greedy algorithm that loses. You revert to zero-shot plus the schema.

Do not move a tagger onto this model "for quality". Route simple work back. Effort is a cost control, not a vibe.

## Interview trap

Do not paste a chat-model CoT script onto a reasoning model. Goal, constraints, schema, effort knob, enough max output so hidden tokens cannot eat the answer. Few-shot traces can pin a worse algorithm — test zero-shot first. Empty long-wait answers are usually a cap problem. Do not put a tagger on this model 'for quality'.
keyPoints: State goal, constraints, and output shape; do not script the steps.
Skip redundant "think step by step" on models that already think.
Hidden reasoning tokens are billed and can consume max output.
Tune the effort/budget setting against quality, cost, and latency.
Few-shot traces can over-constrain; test before you keep them.
Do not use a reasoning model for simple high-volume tagging.

questions.q: How does prompting a reasoning model differ from prompting a standard chat model?
questions.a: Be direct about goal, constraints, and output format. Avoid scripting steps or stacking CoT. Use the effort setting, allow enough output tokens, and test whether examples help.

questions.q: A reasoning-model call waits a long time and returns an empty or cut-off answer. Likely cause?
questions.a: Internal reasoning tokens used up the max-output budget. Raise the limit or lower effort, and log reasoning-token usage.

questions.q: Should you paste a long chain-of-thought example into a reasoning-model prompt?
questions.a: Usually not first. Examples can pin a worse method. Try zero-shot with a schema; if you add a shot, show the final object, not a fake monologue.

questions.q: What knob trades accuracy for cost on these models?
questions.a: The provider's effort, budget, or thinking setting. Treat it like a cost control and A/B it on your eval, rather than adding more prose.

questions.q: Your tagging pipeline moved to a reasoning model "for quality" and p95 exploded. What do you do?
questions.a: Move simple tags back to a standard model; reserve the reasoning model (or high effort) for the hard slice the eval actually needs.

chain-of-thought-vs-hidden-reasoning.explain:
## What it is

**Chain-of-thought (CoT)** is **visible** intermediate text you asked the model to write in the output. **Hidden reasoning** is intermediate work a reasoning model keeps in a separate channel (or does not return). Both spend tokens on thinking. They differ in what **you** can see, log, and debug — and in what you should show a user.

Use visible steps when you need to debug a prompt or teach a standard chat model to work before answering. Use hidden reasoning when the product should not expose scratch work, when the provider already thinks internally, or when you do not want users to treat a fluent essay as an explanation.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, leaking CoT to customers creates two problems: it looks like a justification you may not be able to stand behind, and it can contain policy text or tool traces you never meant to show. Hidden reasoning avoids that but makes prompt debugging harder — you only see the final object. Many teams keep visible scratchpads in **internal** traces and send users only the final field.

Interviewers will ask when you want visible steps. Say: debugging, teaching a non-reasoning model, or a short plan you will validate in code. Say when you do not: user-facing answers, compliance narratives, or when a reasoning model already thinks.

## How it works + one small example

Pattern for a chat model you must debug:

```
<scratch>
... short bullets the eval can ignore ...
</scratch>
{"answer": "...", "confidence": "low|med|high"}
```

You log `<scratch>` internally. The API response to the client is the JSON only.

Pattern for a reasoning model: no `<scratch>` in the user-visible schema. If the provider offers a thinking summary for developers, store it on the trace with access control. Do not forward it to the UI by default.

Do not ask a reasoning model to "repeat your hidden thoughts". That fights the product design and can violate the provider's intended interface.

## Failure modes

1. **Showing CoT as an explanation.** A wrong answer with a beautiful proof still ships. Score the answer; treat the essay as debug.

2. **Parsing the wrong channel.** Your code reads the scratchpad because the JSON failed. Now a user sees internal notes. Fail closed to a default.

3. **Double thinking.** Visible CoT plus hidden effort, no gain. Pick one.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Visible chain-of-thought is for debugging and for chat models that need workspace. Hidden reasoning is for models that already think, and I do not show either to users as an official explanation. I parse a final schema field and I log scratch work on an internal trace.
## Worked scenario

A chat-model classifier needs workspace on borderline tickets. You ask for a short `<scratch>` then JSON. You log scratch internally and strip it before the client. A PM wants to show scratch as "the reason". You refuse: unfaithful, and it can leak policy text. If they need a user-facing reason, you write a separate checked field.

On a reasoning model you do not ask it to reprint hidden thoughts. You request the final schema and store any vendor thinking-summary on an access-controlled trace.

If your parser falls back to printing the pad when JSON fails, users see internal notes. Fail to a default instead. Double thinking (visible CoT plus high effort) is a bill with no eval gain.

## Interview trap

Visible steps are for debug and for chat models that need workspace. Hidden reasoning is for models that already think. Do not show either to users as an official explanation — traces can be unfaithful and leaky. Parse a final field. If JSON fails, do not print the scratchpad to the client. Do not ask a reasoning model to reprint hidden thoughts.
keyPoints: CoT is visible workspace; hidden reasoning stays in a provider channel.
Use visible steps to debug or to force work-before-answer on chat models.
Do not show scratch work to users as a trustworthy explanation.
Log scratch internally; send clients only the final schema field.
Avoid stacking visible CoT on a model that already thinks internally.
Fluent proofs can hide a wrong final answer; score them separately.

questions.q: When do you want visible chain-of-thought versus hidden reasoning?
questions.a: Visible when you are debugging or when a chat model needs to work before answering. Hidden when the model already thinks internally or when users must not see scratch work.

questions.q: A product manager wants to display the model's steps as the "reason for the decision". What is the risk?
questions.a: The steps can be unfaithful or leak prompt/policy text. Use them for debug; write a separate, validated justification if you need a user-facing reason.

questions.q: Your parser falls back to printing the scratchpad when JSON fails. Why is that bad?
questions.a: Users see internal notes and possibly secrets. Fail to a safe default object and keep scratch on an internal-only trace.

questions.q: Should you ask a reasoning model to reprint its hidden thoughts in the answer?
questions.a: No. That fights the interface, can leak channels you should not expose, and usually wastes tokens. Request the final schema only.

questions.q: How do you keep CoT useful for engineers without showing it to customers?
questions.a: Put it in a tagged block, log that block on the server trace, and strip it before the client response. Parse only the final object.

scratchpads-and-intermediate-json.explain:
## What it is

A **scratchpad** is a short, structured place the model writes **before** the final answer: a plan, a list of quoted spans, a set of intermediate fields. **Intermediate JSON** is the same idea with a schema you can check in code (`{"plan": [...], "needs": [...]}` then `{"answer": ...}`). You ask for the pad so **you** can see whether the work is sane, not so the user can read a diary.

This is lighter than a full multi-call decomposition and heavier than a bare answer. It is the right middle when one call should stay one call, but you refuse to trust a lone paragraph.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, "the model said 42" is not debuggable. "The model listed three discounts, applied them in the wrong order, then said 42" is. Intermediate fields turn a black box into something you can unit-test: did it quote a real span? did it list the constraints? did it leave `unknown` when a field was missing?

Interviewers will ask how you check work without a second model. A scratchpad plus a schema is the answer. They may also ask what happens if the pad is fluent and the answer is wrong — you score both, and you do not ship on pad quality alone.

## How it works + one small example

Ask for a **small** pad. Long essays become the new failure mode.

```
Return JSON with this shape:
{
  "quotes": [string],      // verbatim spans from the doc, or []
  "missing": [string],     // fields not in the doc
  "result": {"vendor": string|null, "total_cents": int|null}
}
If a field is not supported by a quote, it must be null.
```

Your code checks: every quote is a substring of the document; `result` fields that are non-null have a quote; `missing` is non-empty when you expected gaps. If the pad fails the check, you retry once or return a safe empty result. You do not parse prose.

For planning: `{"steps": [...], "irreversible": [...]}` before any tool call. For classification: `{"span": "...", "label": "..."}`.

## Failure modes

1. **Essay pads.** You asked for "thoughts" and got 600 tokens of vibes. Constrain keys and lengths (`quotes` max 3, each ≤ 40 tokens).

2. **Scoring only the pad.** A beautiful `plan` with a wrong `result` ships if you only spot-check the plan. Score the result against gold; use the pad for debug and for mechanical checks.

3. **Leaking the pad.** The UI prints `quotes` that include another customer's name. Treat pad fields as internal unless you designed them as user-facing citations.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I ask for a short plan or intermediate JSON before the final fields so I can check quotes, missing fields, or irreversible steps in code. I keep the pad small and schema-bound. I score the final answer separately so a fluent scratchpad cannot hide a wrong result.
## Worked scenario

An extractor invents vendor names. You require `quotes[]` of verbatim spans and `result.vendor` null unless a quote supports it. Code checks `quote in document`. Invented vendors die. You cap `quotes` at three short spans so the pad cannot eat the output budget.

A planner writes `{"steps","irreversible"}` before tools. Code requires a confirm if `send_email` appears. The pad is not a diary; it is a checkable object.

You score `result` against gold separately. A beautiful pad with a wrong total is a fail. Do not let a style judge on the pad ship a wrong answer.

## Interview trap

A pad is a checkable object, not a diary. Prefer `quotes`, `missing`, `result` over 'thoughts'. Mechanical checks: quote in document, null when unsupported, pad length capped. Score the result against gold separately so a fluent pad cannot hide a wrong total. Keep pad fields internal unless they are designed citations.
keyPoints: A scratchpad is a short structured workspace you can check in code.
Prefer a few typed keys over an open "thoughts" essay.
Mechanical checks: quotes must be real substrings; null when unsupported.
Score the final answer separately from the pad.
Keep pad fields internal unless they are designed as citations.
Cap list lengths so the pad cannot eat the output budget.

questions.q: Why ask for intermediate JSON instead of only the final answer?
questions.a: So you can check the work: quotes exist, fields are supported, plans list irreversible steps. A lone final field is not debuggable.

questions.q: How would you stop an extractor from inventing a vendor name?
questions.a: Require a `quotes` array of verbatim spans and a rule that a non-null vendor must have a supporting quote. If the check fails, return null or retry once.

questions.q: The pad is excellent and the result is wrong. Your dashboard is green. What did you measure?
questions.a: You scored the scratchpad, not the answer. Split the metrics: pad-check pass rate versus result correctness against gold.

questions.q: What belongs in a planning scratchpad before tools run?
questions.a: A short step list and an explicit `irreversible` (or similar) field so code can require confirmation before email, pay, or delete.

questions.q: Why cap the size of a scratchpad?
questions.a: Unbounded "thoughts" consume output tokens, raise latency, and become uncheckable prose. Typed short lists stay testable.

plan-then-execute.explain:
## What it is

**Plan-then-execute** is a decomposition where the first artefact is a **plan object** and the second is **action**. You split them when the task uses **tools**, **multiple sources**, or **irreversible** effects (send, pay, delete, post). The plan can be checked — by code, by a second model, or by a human — before anything with a side effect runs.

This is different from a scratchpad in one call. Here you **stop**. You do not let a single generation both decide "email the CFO" and call the mail tool.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is how you keep agents from being one prompt away from an incident. A browsing agent that plans "1) open page 2) extract price 3) email finance" can have step 3 stripped by policy before any SMTP happens. A migration agent can show the ordered statements and wait.

Interviewers will give you an agent with tools and wait. If you let the model call `send_email` in the same breath as the plan, you missed the point. Say: plan schema, validate, confirm irreversible steps, then execute with allow-listed arguments.

## How it works + one small example

```
# call 1 — no side-effect tools bound
{"goal": "notify billing about double charge",
 "steps": [
   {"action": "retrieve", "args": {"ticket_id": "T-19"}},
   {"action": "draft_email", "args": {"to": "billing@acme.com"}},
   {"action": "send_email", "args": {"to": "billing@acme.com"}}
 ],
 "irreversible": ["send_email"]}
```

Code checks: `to` is on an allow-list; `send_email` is marked irreversible so a human (or the user) must tick; retrieve may run automatically. Call 2 binds only the next allowed tool with arguments you copied from the validated plan, not from a new free-form thought.

If the plan is infeasible or out of scope, you stop and say so. You do not "be helpful" by executing a different plan.

## Failure modes

1. **Fake split.** The execute prompt can invent new steps. Bind tools narrowly and reject actions not in the approved plan.

2. **Plan with side-effect tools already attached.** The model "plans" by doing. Bind no irreversible tools on the plan call.

3. **No confirmation UX.** You have an `irreversible` field and nobody looks at it. The field is decoration. Wire it to a tick.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

When a task has tools or irreversible actions I split plan from execute. The plan is a schema I can check; send, pay, and delete wait for an explicit confirm. The execute step may only run approved actions with allow-listed arguments.
## Worked scenario

An agent can retrieve a ticket and send email. Call 1 binds no send tool and returns a plan with `irreversible: ["send_email"]`. Code allow-lists `to` and waits for a tick. Call 2 copies those args; it cannot invent a new recipient. If the plan is out of scope you stop. You do not "be helpful" by executing a different plan.

A fake split — execute prompt can add steps — is how incidents happen. Reject actions not in the approved plan. If `irreversible` is never shown to a human, the field is decoration. Wire the tick.

This is heavier than a scratchpad in one call. Use it when tools or side effects exist, not for a single extract.

## Interview trap

When tools or side effects exist, stop after the plan. Bind no irreversible tools on the plan call. Execute may only run approved steps with allow-listed args copied from the plan. `irreversible` without a tick is decoration. If the plan is out of scope, stop — do not execute a 'helpful' substitute. This is heavier than a one-call scratchpad; use it when SMTP exists.
keyPoints: Split planning from doing when tools, many sources, or side effects exist.
The plan call should not bind irreversible tools.
Validate the plan object, then execute only approved steps.
Email, pay, delete, and post wait for an explicit confirmation.
Reject execute-time steps that were not in the approved plan.
If the plan is out of scope, stop; do not silently do something else.

questions.q: When do you split plan-then-execute instead of using one call?
questions.a: When the task uses tools, multiple sources, or irreversible actions such as email, pay, delete, or post. The plan must be checkable before side effects run.

questions.q: Design the two calls for an agent that can retrieve a ticket and send email.
questions.a: Call 1 binds no send tool and returns a plan with steps and an `irreversible` list. Code allow-lists the recipient and requires a confirm. Call 2 binds send only with those validated args.

questions.q: The execute step sends to a new address that was not in the plan. What failed?
questions.a: Execute was allowed to invent arguments. Copy args from the approved plan, allow-list recipients in code, and reject extras.

questions.q: Why bind no irreversible tools on the planning call?
questions.a: Otherwise the model can perform the action while "planning". Planning must be side-effect free.

questions.q: The plan marks send_email as irreversible but the product never asks the user. What is missing?
questions.a: The field is not wired to a confirmation UX or reviewer tick. The split is incomplete until that tick gates the execute call.

when-decomposition-increases-error.explain:
## What it is

**Decomposition increases error** when you add hops to a task that was already a single mapping: extract-and-label, rewrite, format. Each hop is a chance to **drop a field**, rename a key, or summarise away a number. The last hop then writes a confident answer from an incomplete object. More architecture, worse accuracy.

The warning sign is a pipeline that "looks clean" and a gold set that got worse after you split. Simple tasks want one schema-backed call, not a ceremony.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, well-meaning refactors turn a 94% extractor into an 88% system because hop 2 "normalises" names and hop 3 drops nulls. Interviewers will push you to decompose everything. The senior move is to refuse when the single prompt already meets the bar, and to show a field-level diff that proves the extra hop lost data.

This pairs with the earlier note. You should be able to argue both directions.

## How it works + one small example

A bad split:

```
1) summarise the invoice
2) extract fields from the summary
```

The summary dropped the cents. Extraction is now faithfully wrong. The correct design is: extract from the source document in one call, with nulls allowed.

Another bad split: classify sentiment, then map sentiment to a label list in a second call that is allowed to "fix" the first. You now have two places to disagree with gold.

Rule of thumb: if you cannot name a **check** that hop N performs which hop N-1 could not, delete hop N. If hop N only restates, it is noise.

When you do split, pass **structured fields forward**, not prose summaries, and assert that required keys still exist after each hop.

## Failure modes

1. **Summary bridges.** Prose between structured stages is a data-loss machine.

2. **Optional hops that become load-bearing.** A "nice to have" rewriter starts changing amounts. Pin the writer to a template that cannot introduce numbers.

3. **No field-level eval.** You only score the final paragraph, so you never see that `total_cents` died on hop 2.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I do not decompose simple extract-and-label work. Each hop can drop a field. If I split, I pass structured objects, I assert keys between hops, and I will revert the split if a field-level eval gets worse.
## Worked scenario

Someone "cleans up" invoice extraction by summarising first, then extracting from the summary. Cents disappear. You revert to one schema-backed extract from the source. Field-level F1 recovers. The architecture looked cleaner and was worse.

A second hop that only restates the first is noise. If you cannot name the check it adds, delete it. When you must split, pass structured objects and assert keys after each hop. Score per-field metrics or you will not see that `total_cents` died on hop 2.

In an interview, refuse to decompose a task that already meets the bar. That refusal is a signal, not a lack of ambition.

## Interview trap

Summarise-then-extract is the classic self-own: cents die in the summary. Extract from the source. Score field-level F1 before and after a split. If you cannot name the check a hop adds, delete the hop. Refusing to decompose a task that already meets the bar is a signal in an interview, not a lack of ambition.
## On a real team

A 'cleanup' PR that inserts a summary hop will look architectural in review and will fail field-level eval. Require the before/after per-key table in the PR. If `total_cents` or a negation moved, revert the hop. Teach the team that passing structured objects and asserting keys is the only split that is allowed to merge. Ceremony without that table is a regression dressed as design. Keep a one-line heuristic on the wiki: no hop without a named check the previous hop could not do.
keyPoints: Extra hops on simple mappings drop fields and add latency.
Do not extract from a summary of the source; extract from the source.
If you cannot name a check a hop adds, delete the hop.
Pass structured objects between stages, not prose bridges.
Score field-level metrics so a lost key is visible.
Be ready to refuse decomposition in an interview when the bar is already met.

questions.q: When does decomposition increase error?
questions.a: On simple extract-and-label or rewrite tasks, where each extra hop can drop or distort a field. A single schema-backed call is safer.

questions.q: A pipeline summarises an invoice then extracts totals from the summary. Totals are wrong. Why?
questions.a: The summary discarded cents or currency. Extract from the original document in one hop; do not interpose prose.

questions.q: What test tells you a split made things worse?
questions.a: A field-level eval (per-key F1 or exact match) on the same gold set, compared before and after the split — not only a vibe read of the final paragraph.

questions.q: Give a rule of thumb for deleting a hop.
questions.a: If you cannot name a check that hop performs which the previous hop could not, it is restating and should go.

questions.q: You must split for other reasons. How do you limit data loss?
questions.a: Pass structured objects, assert required keys after each hop, and forbid later hops from inventing numbers not present in the structured input.

measuring-reasoning-quality.explain:
## What it is

**Measuring reasoning quality** means you score the **final answer** and the **plan or scratchpad** as **separate** metrics. A fluent chain that ends on the wrong number is a failure that a "looks thoughtful" judge will miss. A terse correct answer with an empty pad can be a success you should keep, especially on a simple task.

You need this the moment you ask for steps, plans, or hidden thinking. Otherwise you will optimise for essay quality — longer, nicer, more expensive — and ship wrong totals.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, LLM-as-judge evals love well-written rationales. Teams then raise temperature and effort to get prettier traces while field accuracy falls. Splitting the scoreboard (answer exact-match / numeric tolerance / schema pass vs pad-check / plan-feasibility) stops that.

Interviewers will ask how you know a reasoning prompt helped. "The steps looked better" is a fail. "Final-answer score rose and pad-check still passes; tokens are within budget" is a pass.

## How it works + one small example

Define two families of checks:

- **Answer metrics:** exact match, numeric tolerance, rubric on the user-visible field, schema validity.
- **Process metrics:** quotes are substrings; plan steps are in an allow-list; no irreversible action without a flag; pad length under a cap.

```
case 14
  answer_ok: false   # 42 vs gold 37
  pad_ok:    true    # quotes real, steps legal
  tokens:    900
```

A change that lifts `pad_ok` and drops `answer_ok` is a regression. A change that lifts `answer_ok` and increases tokens is a trade you can accept if it clears the bar.

For hidden reasoning, you may only have answer metrics plus usage. That is fine. Do not invent a judge that scores tokens you cannot see.

Use low temperature or multiple samples when you measure, and compare on the **same** cases. Do not judge from one cherry-picked trace.

## Failure modes

1. **Judge captures style.** "Well reasoned" correlates with length. Rubrics must ask about the answer, or use exact match.

2. **One number for everything.** A blended score lets a pretty pad hide a wrong total. Keep the columns.

3. **No cost column.** You will crown a reasoning model that is 1 point better and 8× slower without noticing.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I score the final answer and the plan separately so fluent steps cannot hide a wrong result. Process checks are mechanical when I can make them — real quotes, legal steps. I look at tokens and latency next to those scores, and I do not ship a prettier pad that missed gold.
## Worked scenario

A judge loves long traces. You raise effort; traces get prettier; totals get worse. You split the scoreboard: `answer_ok` vs `pad_ok` vs tokens. The next change that lifts pad and drops answer is reverted. You switch the primary metric to exact match on the total and keep pad checks mechanical (quotes are substrings, steps in an allow-list).

For hidden reasoning you only have answer metrics plus usage. You do not invent a judge over text you cannot see.

Keep a cost column. A 1-point gain at 8× latency is a product decision, not an automatic ship. Compare on the same cases, not one cherry-picked essay.

## Interview trap

Judges love long traces. Split `answer_ok` and `pad_ok` and tokens. A prettier pad with a wrong total is a fail. Prefer mechanical process checks. Hidden reasoning is measured by the answer and by usage, not by a fake essay score. A 1-point gain at 8× latency is a product call, not an automatic ship. Same cases, not one cherry-picked proof.
keyPoints: Score the final answer and the plan/scratchpad as separate columns.
A fluent wrong answer is a fail, even if the pad looks excellent.
Prefer mechanical process checks (quotes, allow-listed steps) over style judges.
Keep a cost/latency column so you do not crown an 8× slower 1-point gain.
Compare on the same cases; do not judge from one trace.
Hidden reasoning is measured by the answer and by usage, not by a fake essay score.

questions.q: Why score the plan and the final answer separately?
questions.a: Because a fluent plan can accompany a wrong result. A blended score or a style judge will hide that. Two columns make the regression visible.

questions.q: Your LLM judge prefers longer traces and accuracy fell. What happened?
questions.a: The judge is scoring style or length, not the answer. Switch the primary metric to exact match or a rubric on the final field; keep pad checks mechanical.

questions.q: What process checks can you run without another model?
questions.a: Quote-is-substring, required keys present, steps in an allow-list, pad length under a cap, schema valid. These catch a lot before you pay for a judge.

questions.q: You cannot see hidden reasoning tokens' text. What do you measure?
questions.a: Final-answer quality, schema pass rate, and usage/latency. Do not invent a judge over text you do not have.

questions.q: A new prompt lifts pad_ok and drops answer_ok. Do you ship it?
questions.a: No. That is a reasoning-quality regression dressed as process improvement. Revert or keep iterating until the answer column recovers.

debugging-a-reasoning-prompt.explain:
## What it is

**Debugging a reasoning prompt** is a short playbook for when traces ramble, answers are wrong, or latency explodes. The three moves you should try on purpose, in roughly this order: **drop forced step-by-step**, **add a schema** (or a smaller scratchpad), or **switch model family** (standard ↔ reasoning, or a different provider). Then re-run the **same** eval. Do not add another paragraph of "be careful" first.

Rambling is a symptom. The causes are usually: you asked for an essay, you stacked visible CoT on a reasoning model, you put the answer first, or this model family is the wrong tool for the task.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, reasoning bugs eat days because the output looks busy. A playbook turns that into a 30-minute experiment. Interviewers will hand you a 800-token ramble and a wrong integer. If you start line-editing the essay, you fail. If you say "remove CoT, pin a schema, try a non-reasoning model on this extract-heavy set", you pass.

## How it works + one small example

Playbook:

1. Read the **rendered** prompt and the raw output, including finish reason and token counts.
2. If the trace is an essay: delete "think step by step" / long pad; keep a 3-key JSON scratch or none.
3. If the answer is unstructured: add a schema and parse only that field.
4. If you are on a reasoning model and the task is extract/classify: switch to a standard model (or lower effort).
5. If you are on a standard model and the task is multi-constraint math/planning: try a reasoning model or a plan-then-execute split.
6. Change **one** of these per experiment. Re-run the same set. Keep or revert.

```
# before
think carefully about every possibility...
# after
Return {"total_cents": int|null}. If any input is missing, null.
```

Also check truncation: rambling plus a low max-output looks like "the model gave up". It hit the cap.

## Failure modes

1. **Patch-per-ramble.** You add "do not ramble" ten times. The prompt is now a pile of mood. Reset to a short contract.

2. **Changing model and prompt together.** You will not know what worked. One variable.

3. **Debugging on one example.** You fix the demo and break the set. Always the same suite.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

When traces ramble I drop forced step-by-step, I pin a small schema, or I switch model family — one change at a time on the same eval. I check truncation and token counts first. I do not line-edit an 800-token essay.
## Worked scenario

An 800-token ramble ends mid-JSON. Finish reason is `length`. You do not line-edit the essay. You drop forced CoT, pin a three-key schema, and raise max output (or lower effort). You change one of those at a time on the same 40 cases.

A kitchen-sink deploy that also swapped model family "fixed it" and you cannot say why. You roll back and apply one variable.

Adding "please do not ramble" ten times is a mood pile. Reset to a short contract. If the task is extract, switch off the reasoning model. If it is multi-constraint math on a chat model, try a reasoning model or a plan-then-execute split — still one change per run.

## Interview trap

Do not line-edit an 800-token ramble. Check finish_reason and tokens first. Then drop forced CoT, pin a schema, or switch family — one variable, same eval. Kitchen-sink deploys cannot be attributed. 'Please do not ramble' is a mood sentence. Reset to a short contract. Extract work belongs on a standard model.
## On a real team

Make the playbook a runbook in the repo: check finish_reason, then one of {drop CoT, tighten schema, switch family}, same eval, keep or revert. Ban 'please do not ramble' as a commit message. If someone changed model and prompt together, the first action is rollback, not celebration. Put the three moves in the on-call doc so a 2 a.m. ramble does not become a 4-hour essay edit.
keyPoints: Playbook: drop forced CoT, add a schema, or switch model family.
Change one variable per experiment and re-run the same eval set.
Check finish reason and token counts; rambling often hits max output.
Do not stack visible CoT on a reasoning model that is already thinking.
Reset a mood-pile prompt to a short contract instead of adding "don't ramble".
Never debug reasoning quality on a single cherry-picked trace.

questions.q: What three moves do you try when a reasoning prompt rambles?
questions.a: Drop forced step-by-step, add or tighten a schema (or a smaller scratchpad), or switch model family / effort. Then re-run the same eval.

questions.q: The model writes 800 tokens and the JSON is cut off. First check?
