| machine only | JSON / schema | parse, types, enums |
| human only, no reuse | Markdown | headings, emphasis, links |
| comparison of a few rows | Markdown table **or** JSON rendered as a table | tables rot if too wide |
| both | JSON then render | one source of truth |

```
# machine path
Return only {"items":[{"name":string,"price_cents":int}]}

# human path (separate prompt id)
Write a Markdown list. Each item is bold name then price. No table.
```

If you must show a table to a human, cap columns (3–5) and rows, and say what to do with overflow ("first 8 rows, then a count of the rest"). Wide tables wrap and hallucinate cells.

Do not ask for JSON inside a Markdown fence unless you have to; fences are one more thing to strip. Structured-output APIs remove the fence problem.

## Failure modes

1. **"Any structured format".** You will write a union parser and still lose.

2. **Tables as a database.** The model invents alignment and drops a cell. Use JSON for data.

3. **One prompt, two consumers.** The Slack copy and the pipeline fight. Two prompt ids, or JSON + renderer.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I pick the format for the consumer: JSON for code, Markdown for humans, and if I need both I generate JSON and render. I show one example of the chosen format. I do not let a model invent a table when I need data I can test.
## Worked scenario

Slack and a billing pipeline share a prompt that "sometimes tables". You split: the pipeline gets schema JSON; Slack gets a renderer in code. The union parser is deleted. A 12-column Markdown table that dropped cells is replaced by JSON rows and a 4-column view.

You show exactly one example of the chosen format. Two formats in the shots taught drift.

"Any structured format is fine" is two specs. Name the consumer first. If both consume it, one object, two presentations.

## Interview trap

Name the consumer. Machines get JSON, humans get Markdown, both get JSON plus a renderer. 'Sometimes a table' is two parsers. Wide tables drop cells. Show one example of the chosen format. Two formats in the shots teach drift. Schema APIs beat fenced JSON in a blog post.
## On a real team

A format field on the prompt registry: json | markdown | json+render. Slack and pipelines cannot share a 'flexible' prompt id. Table generation is banned above a column cap. Renderers are tested with injected pipes and backticks so the model never owns escaping. One example fixture per format, checked in.

## Remember

One consumer, one format, one example. Two consumers, one JSON object and a renderer you test. 'Flexible structured' is how weekly regexes are born.
keyPoints: Name the consumer first, then pick JSON, Markdown, or a table.
One primary format per prompt version; show one example of it.
For dual consumers, generate JSON and render presentation in code.
Wide tables wrap and drop cells; cap columns and rows.
"JSON or a table" is two specs and two parsers.
Prefer schema APIs over fenced JSON in a Markdown blob.

questions.q: How do you choose between JSON, Markdown, and tables?
questions.a: By consumer: machines get JSON, humans get Markdown, comparisons can be a small table. If both consume it, emit JSON and render.

questions.q: A Slack bot and a billing pipeline share one prompt that "sometimes tables". What do you do?
questions.a: Split prompt ids or emit JSON once and render Slack Markdown in code. A union format is not a design.

questions.q: A 12-column Markdown table is missing cells. Why was the format wrong?
questions.a: Wide tables are a bad generation target. Store rows as JSON and render a narrower view, or cap columns.

questions.q: Why show exactly one example of the chosen format?
questions.a: The model imitates the demonstration. Two formats in the shots teach drift. One example is the spec in action.

questions.q: When is a Markdown table acceptable?
questions.a: Human-only output, few columns and rows, overflow rule stated. Not when another system must parse the cells.

repair-loops-after-invalid-output.explain:
## What it is

A **repair loop** is: generate, **validate** in your code, if invalid send the **error back once**, generate again, if still invalid **fail to a default** you own. It is how you absorb the remaining 1–5% after prompting and (ideally) a schema. It is not `while True`. Infinite repair is an outage and a bill.

The repair message should be specific: the validator's error, not "please try again". The second call should still use the schema. The default should be safe (abstain object, empty list, escalate flag), not a guessed record.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, repair done right turns a flaky 97% into a boring 99.9% plus a metric for the rest. Repair done wrong retries a poisoned input 20 times, or "repairs" into a hallucinated vendor. Interviewers will ask you to walk generate → validate → repair → fallback. That walk-through is the next note's cousin; this one is the loop policy.

## How it works + one small example

```
def complete(inp):
    out = generate(inp, schema)
    ok, err = validate(out)
    if ok:
        return out
    out = generate(inp, schema, note=f"Validation failed: {err}. Return a valid object.")
    ok, err = validate(out)
    if ok:
        return out
    log("repair_exhausted", err)
    return DEFAULT  # {"label":"other","reply":None} or similar
```

Count repairs in metrics. If a prompt version needs repair on 20% of calls, fix the prompt or schema; do not celebrate the retry. Cap total elapsed time. Do not repair when the input itself is empty — return the empty default immediately.

## Failure modes

1. **Unbounded while.** A provider blip plus a bad validator becomes a cost incident.

2. **Vague repair.** "That wasn't JSON" without the error. The second sample repeats the first.

3. **Default that looks real.** A fabricated vendor in the fallback. Defaults must be obviously abstaining.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I validate in code, I send the validator error back once, and I fail to a safe default if it still does not parse. I never loop forever. A high repair rate is a signal to fix the prompt or schema, not a reason to retry harder.
## Worked scenario

Repair said "please try again" and the second sample matched the first. You include the validator error (`missing reason`, `label not in enum`) and keep the schema on the retry. You cap at one attempt and 2s extra. DEFAULT is `{label: other, needs_human: true}`, not a guessed vendor.

Repair rate is 20%. You treat that as a contract bug, not a success. Empty inputs skip repair and go straight to empty status.

Unbounded while plus a provider blip is a cost incident. The loop is a last 1% net, not the product.

## Interview trap

Validate, send the real error once, fail to an abstaining default. 'Try again' without the error repeats the first sample. 20% repair rate means the contract is wrong. Do not repair empty inputs. The fallback must not look like a successful row. Keep the schema on the retry.
## On a real team

The client library implements one-shot repair with the validator error and a shared DEFAULT. Features cannot override the attempt cap. Repair_rate alerts at 5%. Empty inputs short-circuit. On-call knows that a spike is a contract regression, not a reason to raise the cap to three. Fallbacks are reviewed like error types.

## Remember

One honest retry with the validator's words, then a default that cannot be mistaken for success. A high repair rate is a pager, not a feature. Empty inputs skip the dance.
keyPoints: Validate, repair once with the real error, then fail to a safe default.
Never unbounded while-retry; cap attempts and wall time.
The fallback must abstain, not look like a real record.
A high repair rate means the prompt or schema is wrong.
Do not repair empty or out-of-scope inputs; default immediately.
Keep the schema on the repair call; do not fall back to free prose.

questions.q: What is the allowed repair policy after invalid output?
questions.a: Validate, send the validator error back once, validate again, then fail to a default your code owns. No unbounded loops.

questions.q: The repair prompt says "please try again" and the second output matches the first. Why?
questions.a: The model was not told what failed. Include the validator error (missing key, illegal enum) and keep the schema attached.

questions.q: Design a safe DEFAULT for a ticket classifier.
questions.a: Something like {"label":"other","reply":null,"needs_human":true} that cannot be mistaken for a successful billing decision.

questions.q: Repair rate is 20%. Is the loop working?
questions.a: It is papering over a bad contract. Fix the prompt, examples, or schema; use repair as a last 1% net, not as the product.

questions.q: Why keep structured output enabled on the repair call?
questions.a: Free-form repair reintroduces fences and preambles. The second sample should be at least as constrained as the first.

provider-structured-output-apis.explain:
## What it is

**Provider structured-output APIs** constrain decoding so the model can only emit tokens that fit a **JSON schema** (or a grammar / function-call signature). That is a different mechanism from "please return JSON". The model is not hoped into obedience; the decoder refuses illegal tokens. Prefer this whenever a parser is downstream.

Details differ by vendor — `response_format`, tool/function calling, strict schema modes — and they change. Read the current official docs. The design does not: define a schema, generate under it, still validate on your side (providers have bugs and limits), still have a default.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the difference between a 92% parse rate and a 99.8% parse rate at the same prompt quality. Interviewers will ask "JSON please vs schema mode". You should say schema-constrained decoding, plus your own validator, plus one repair, plus a fallback. You should also say what schemas cannot do: they cannot make a vendor name true.

## How it works + one small example

```
schema = {
  "type": "object",
  "additionalProperties": False,
  "required": ["label", "reason"],
  "properties": {
    "label": {"enum": ["billing", "bug", "how-to", "other"]},
    "reason": {"type": "string"},
  },
}
out = client.generate(messages, response_format=schema)
```

Keep schemas tight: `additionalProperties: false`, enums instead of free strings, numbers for money (cents), null allowed where abstain is legal. Avoid exotic JSON Schema features your provider silently drops. Log schema-validation failures separately from model errors.

When a schema is too tight for a hard reasoning task, add an optional `notes` string, or split plan/answer, rather than abandoning constraints.

## Failure modes

1. **Hope-driven JSON.** You skipped the API because the playground looked clean.

2. **Unvalidated trust.** You assume the provider always matches the schema. Still run zod/pydantic.

3. **Over-wide schema.** Everything is a string. You paid for a feature you did not use.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I prefer schema-constrained decoding over hoping the model obeys "JSON please". I still validate on my side and I still have a default. A schema enforces shape, not truth.
## Worked scenario

You switch a classifier to the provider's schema mode with tight enums and `additionalProperties: false`. Parse rate jumps. You still run pydantic and keep a default. A week later a provider edge case emits an extra key; local validation catches it.

A schema that types everything as string wasted the feature. You use ints for cents and enums for labels. You read the current official docs for the flag name rather than a remembered beta.

If a hard task needs workspace, you add `notes` or split plan/answer. You do not abandon constraints or hope-driven "JSON please".

## Interview trap

Constrained decoding is a different mechanism from hoping. Still validate locally. Tight enums, no extra keys, null for abstain. Read current official docs for the flag name. A stringly-typed schema wastes the feature. Schemas do not make facts true. Notes field if workspace is needed.
## On a real team

Wrap the vendor flag in one module so a docs change is one file. Local validation is mandatory in that module. Schema lints reject all-string objects and missing additionalProperties false. When a provider bug ships, the fallback path is already tested. A wiki line points at current official docs, not a Slack screenshot of a beta parameter.
keyPoints: Constrained decoding is a different mechanism from prompting for JSON.
Prefer provider structured-output or function-call schemas when a parser sits downstream.
Still validate locally; still have a fallback.
Keep schemas tight: enums, no extra keys, null where abstain is legal.
A schema cannot make a fact true.
Read current official docs; flag names differ by provider and change.

questions.q: Why prefer schema-constrained decoding over "please return JSON"?
questions.a: The decoder can only emit legal tokens, so parse rates jump. Prompting is probabilistic and still produces fences and preambles.

questions.q: You enabled structured output. Do you skip your own validator?
questions.a: No. Providers have limits and bugs. Local validation plus a default remains part of the contract.

questions.q: A schema types every field as string and quality did not improve. What was wasted?
questions.a: The constraint. Use enums, integers, booleans, and additionalProperties false so illegal values cannot be sampled.

questions.q: When might a very rigid schema hurt a hard task?
questions.a: When the model needs workspace before committing. Add a notes field or split plan then answer, rather than dropping constraints entirely.

questions.q: Where do you look up the exact flag name for this feature?
questions.a: The provider's current official docs (OpenAI structured outputs, Anthropic, Gemini, Azure). Do not rely on a remembered beta parameter.

refusal-and-empty-output-handling.explain:
## What it is

**Refusal and empty-output handling** means you define the **exact object or label** to return when the model must **abstain**: out of scope, unsafe, insufficient evidence, empty input, or a policy refusal. "Just refuse" produces a snowflake paragraph that your parser cannot see. A first-class `refused` / `empty` / `unknown` path produces a branch your product can run.

This is the output-side twin of the system-prompt missing-info rule. The prompt says when to abstain; the schema says **how abstention looks**.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, mixed "I'm sorry I can't…" strings leak into tables, break types, and sometimes contain a partial answer after the apology. Interviewers will ask what you return when the model must not answer. Naming a concrete object is the signal.

## How it works + one small example

```
{
  "status": "ok" | "empty" | "refused" | "unknown",
  "label": "billing" | "bug" | "how-to" | "other" | null,
  "reply": string | null,
  "reason": string | null
}
```

Rules:

- Empty input → `status=empty`, all else null.
- Not in document / not sure → `status=unknown`.
- Policy or safety → `status=refused` with a short canned `reason` from an allow-list, not a leaked policy essay.
- Never mix a guessed `label` with `status=refused`.

Your UI maps those statuses to copy you wrote, not to model prose. Your metrics count each status so a spike in `unknown` is visible.

## Failure modes

1. **Refuse in prose, succeed in JSON.** `{label: billing, reply: "I cannot help"}`. Pick one status.

2. **No empty status.** Blank tickets become creative labels.

3. **Leaky refusal reasons.** The model quotes the system prompt. Use a canned reason code (`out_of_scope`, `unsafe`, `insufficient_evidence`).

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I define the exact object to return when the model must abstain — empty, unknown, refused — as first-class status values, and I never mix a guessed label with a refusal. The UI owns the user-facing sentence. Snowflake apologies are not a contract.
## Worked scenario

Refusals were snowflake paragraphs that sometimes contained a partial answer. You add `status: ok|empty|unknown|refused` and force payload fields null when status is not ok. The UI maps `refused/out_of_scope` to a canned shipping-only sentence. Metrics show a spike in `unknown` after a bad retrieval deploy — visible, fixable.

A `{status: refused, label: billing}` object is a bug. Guessed labels cannot ride with refusals. Reason codes are an allow-list (`out_of_scope`, `unsafe`, `insufficient_evidence`) so the model cannot leak the system prompt in `reason`.

## Interview trap

Abstention is a status enum, not a snowflake sorry. Empty, unknown, and refused are different branches. Never emit a guessed label with a refusal. Canned reason codes so the model cannot leak the system prompt. The UI owns the sentence. Metric each status.
## On a real team

Status enums are in a shared package used by API, UI, and eval. A test forbids non-null payloads on non-ok status. Reason codes are an allow-list. Product writes the user sentences. An alert on unknown-rate catches retrieval outages that would otherwise look like 'the model got worse'. Snowflake apologies cannot reach the client.

## Remember

Abstain is a first-class object. Empty is not unknown is not refused. The UI speaks; the model returns a status. Mixed guessed labels on a refusal are bugs, not personality.

Say this: abstain is an object I defined, not a paragraph the model invents. Empty, unknown, and refused are different doors. The UI has the key to each door. That is how parsers and people stay aligned.
keyPoints: Abstention is a first-class status in the schema, not a free-form sorry.
Empty, unknown, and refused are different branches.
Do not emit a guessed label alongside a refusal.
Use canned reason codes; do not leak the system prompt in the reason.
The UI maps statuses to copy you wrote.
Metric each status so a spike in unknown is visible.

questions.q: Why not let the model write a free-form refusal paragraph?
questions.a: Parsers cannot branch on it, it may leak policy text, and it often mixes with a partial answer. A status enum is a contract.

questions.q: Design statuses for a document QA endpoint.
questions.a: ok (answer + citations), unknown (not in document), empty (no question or no doc), refused (out of scope / unsafe). No guessed answer on non-ok.

questions.q: The object is {status: refused, label: billing}. What is wrong?
questions.a: A guessed label leaked through a refusal. Force label=null when status is not ok.

questions.q: Where should the user-facing "I can only help with shipping" sentence live?
questions.a: In your UI (or a tiny canned map), keyed by status/reason. Do not rely on the model to improvise the sentence.

questions.q: What happens if you omit an empty status?
questions.a: Blank inputs get a creative ok answer. Empty is a real production case and needs its own legal object.

temperature-vs-format-reliability.explain:
## What it is

**Temperature** (and related sampling knobs like top-p) controls how boldly the model departs from the most likely next token. Higher temperature increases variety; lower temperature increases repetition of the mode. **Format reliability** — will this parse? — improves as you **lower temperature** and, far more, as you **use a schema**. Temperature is a softness knob. It is not a parser.

When a parser is downstream, start low (often 0 or near 0), enable structured output, and still validate. When you want diverse drafts (marketing, brainstorm), raise temperature on a **prose** prompt that humans will read, not on the object you will `json.loads`.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, people raise temperature to "be more creative" on a classifier and then wonder why enums drift. Interviewers will ask how temperature interacts with JSON. The answer: lower it for machines; do not use it as a substitute for a schema; temperature 0 is still not a guarantee across runs or providers.

## How it works + one small example

```
# classifier / extractor
temperature=0 (or 0.1), schema on, validate

# three marketing subject lines for a human to pick
temperature=0.8, prose, no parser
```

Do not split the difference (0.5) on a parsed path "just in case". If you need diversity **and** a schema (multiple candidate labels), sample n times at low temperature or ask for a list field under the schema — do not turn the knob up and pray the braces survive.

Seeds, when offered, are best-effort. Never document "deterministic" unless you have measured it on your stack. Pin the model version; floating aliases move more than temperature does.

## Failure modes

1. **Creative JSON.** Temperature 0.9 on a tool-call path. Args drift, parsers fail.

2. **Temperature as the only control.** Adding a schema later cuts parse errors more than dropping 0.3 → 0.0 did.

3. **Assuming T=0 is bitwise stable.** It is not, especially across days and providers.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

When a parser is downstream I lower temperature and I use a schema. Temperature only changes sampling softness; it does not enforce braces. I raise temperature on human-read prose, not on objects I will parse, and I never call T=0 a guarantee.
## Worked scenario

A classifier at T=0.8 invents a fifth label. You drop T to 0 and constrain the enum. You do not share that knob with a marketing path that wants three diverse subject lines at T=0.8 in prose.

Someone claims T=0 means you can skip structured output and skip pinning. Quality jumps over a weekend with a clean prompt git. The alias moved. T=0 is not bitwise stable and is not a schema.

A "compromise" 0.5 on a parsed path is indecision. Pick the path's consumer, then the knob.

## Interview trap

Low T plus a schema for parsers. High T for human-read drafts. Do not share one knob. T=0 is not bitwise deterministic and is not a reason to skip a schema or a pin. A weekend quality jump with a clean prompt git is an alias move. A compromise 0.5 on a parsed path is indecision.
## On a real team

Parsed routes default T to 0 in the client and refuse to take 0.5 'just in case'. Prose brainstorm routes are a different helper. Model pins are required on both. A weekend quality jump pages the pin watcher, not the prompt author. Document that T=0 is not bitwise so nobody writes 'deterministic' in a design doc again.

## Remember

Softness and grammar are different knobs. Parsers get low T and a schema. Humans get variety on a different path. Pins move more than 0.1 of temperature. Write that down.
keyPoints: Low temperature + a schema for anything a parser reads.
High temperature is for human-read diversity, not for JSON.
Temperature 0 is not bitwise deterministic across runs or vendors.
A schema fixes format more than shaving 0.3 off temperature.
Do not run a "compromise" 0.5 on a parsed path.
Pin model versions; aliases move behaviour more than small T changes.

questions.q: How should temperature change when a parser is downstream?
questions.a: Lower it (often 0 or near 0) and enable a schema. Temperature alone is not format enforcement.

questions.q: A classifier at T=0.8 sometimes invents a fifth label. What two changes do you make?
questions.a: Drop temperature on that path and constrain the label with an enum schema. Do not add more "only use these labels" sentences first.

questions.q: You want three diverse subject lines and a parsed JSON classifier. How many temperatures?
questions.a: Two paths: high T for the prose drafts a human picks, low T plus schema for the classifier. Do not share one knob.

questions.q: Is temperature 0 enough to skip structured output?
questions.a: No. T=0 still produces preambles and rare malformed objects, and it is not fully deterministic. Use a schema anyway.

questions.q: Quality jumped after a weekend with no prompt change. Temperature was 0. What else drifted?
questions.a: Likely a floating model alias or provider-side change. Pin versions and re-run the golden set; do not blame T.

interview.explain:
## What it is

**Interview: enforce a schema** is a spoken walk-through of the stack your code owns: **generate** under a schema, **validate** locally, **repair once** with the validator error, then a **fallback** that cannot look like a successful record. You are not being asked to recite a vendor flag. You are being asked whether you treat format as an engineering contract.

This is M3.5 condensed into one minute. If you only say "I tell the model to return JSON", you have described a hope. If you name the four steps and what the default looks like, you have described a system.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is a common design question for anyone who has put an LLM in front of a database or a UI state machine. Interviewers listen for: schema-constrained decoding, local validation (zod/pydantic), a one-shot repair, a safe default, logging of parse failures, and the sentence that valid JSON can still be semantically wrong.

## How it works + one small example

Say this, and optionally box it:

1. **Generate** with the provider's structured-output or function-call schema. Tight enums, `additionalProperties` false, nulls for abstain.
2. **Validate** with the same schema in process. Never trust the wire.
3. **Repair** at most once: send the validator error, keep the schema, do not say "try again" without the error.
4. **Fallback**: `{status: "unknown", ...nulls}` or an escalate flag. Not a guessed row.
5. **Observe**: schema_pass, repair_rate, fallback_rate, plus a semantic score.

Mention temperature is low on this path, finish_reason is checked, and a `length` finish is a failure. Mention you will not repair empty inputs.

If they ask about truth: "The schema does not make the vendor name true; grounding and eval do."

## Failure modes

1. **Stopping at step 1.** "We use structured outputs" without validate/fallback. Providers fail.

2. **A fallback that looks successful.** Invented `vendor: Acme` on error. That is worse than throwing.

3. **Forgetting semantics.** You only talk about braces. They will ask about a valid wrong object.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I generate under a schema, I validate in my process, I repair once with the real error, and I fail to a default my code owns — usually an unknown/escalate object, never a guessed row. I log parse failures. A schema enforces shape, not truth.
## Worked scenario

You walk generate → validate → one repair → safe fallback in 45 seconds. You name a default that abstains. You mention low T, `finish_reason=length` as failure, and "valid JSON can still be the wrong vendor". You do not stop at "we use structured outputs".

They ask what you log: schema_pass, repair_rate, fallback_rate, next to a semantic score. They ask about empty input: no repair, empty status immediately.

A fallback that looks like `{vendor: Acme}` on error is worse than throwing. Say that out loud. Shape is not truth.

## Interview trap

Say generate, validate, one repair, safe fallback. Name an abstaining default. Mention length-finish as failure and 'valid JSON can still be the wrong vendor'. Stopping at 'we use structured outputs' skips the system. Log schema_pass, repair_rate, fallback_rate next to a semantic score.
## On a real team

The four-step stack is the library, not a slide. New services cannot call the raw vendor client. Interviewers on your team ask the same walk-through you run in prod: generate, validate, repair once, abstain default, metrics. If a candidate stops at structured outputs, that is the same miss as a service that skipped local validation.
keyPoints: Walk generate → validate → one repair → safe fallback.
Local validation still happens after provider structured output.
The fallback abstains; it does not invent a successful record.
Log schema_pass, repair_rate, and fallback_rate next to semantic scores.
Low temperature and a checked finish_reason belong on this path.
Say out loud: valid JSON can still be the wrong fact.

questions.q: Walk through generate, validate, repair, and fallback as you would in an interview.
questions.a: Generate under a provider schema; validate with the same schema in process; if invalid, one repair call that includes the validator error; if still invalid, return a safe abstain default you own and log it.

questions.q: What must the fallback object look like?
questions.a: Obviously unsuccessful: status=unknown or needs_human=true, payload fields null. Never a plausible invented row.

questions.q: The candidate says "we use structured outputs" and stops. What did they skip?
questions.a: Local validation, a bounded repair, a fallback, and metrics. Provider mode is step one, not the system.

questions.q: How do you answer "what if the JSON is valid but the vendor is wrong"?
questions.a: That is a semantic miss. Ground, allow null, eval field accuracy. The schema did its job; do not tighten JSON further to fix truth.

questions.q: Why mention finish_reason in this walk-through?
questions.a: A length finish is a truncated object and should take the failure/fallback path, not a partial parse that looks like success.

diagnosing-prompt-failures.explain:
## What it is

**Diagnosing prompt failures** means you classify the miss before you edit. Read the **rendered** prompt (after templating), the **raw** output, the finish reason, and a handful of similar failures. Then tag the cause: ambiguous instruction, conflicting constraints, poor examples, missing context, or a weak output spec. Most bad edits happen because someone patched the first theory they liked.

Diagnosis is a habit, not a tool. A spreadsheet of ten failures with tags beats a new paragraph of "never do X".

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, prompt files rot into incident diaries. Each bug adds a never; none of the nevers were checked against the whole set. Interviewers will hand you a bad output and wait. If you start rewriting, you fail. If you ask for the rendered prompt, the gold, and two more failures, you pass.

## How it works + one small example

Checklist:

1. Render the template with the actual variables. Look for empty slots, doubled fences, truncated context.
2. Read finish_reason and token counts. `length` is not a prompt-idea bug.
3. Tag: **ambiguity**, **conflict**, **missing context**, **bad examples**, **weak spec**, plus **input weirdness**.
4. Reproduce at low temperature to separate sampling noise from a systematic miss.
5. Change **one** thing aimed at the tag. Re-run the whole set.

```
# tags on 8 failures
weak spec:     5   → add schema / output section
missing ctx:   2   → retrieval
conflict:      1   → delete "be thorough" vs "JSON only"
```

The majority tag is the first fix. Do not add a rule for the singleton until the pile is gone.

## Failure modes

1. **Editing from memory.** The playground text is not what production rendered. A bad `{{ticket}}` substitution is a common "model is dumb" ticket.

2. **Patch-per-bug.** Five nevers later, new failures appear. Consolidate.

3. **Debugging at high T.** You cannot tell prompt from noise. Drop T for diagnosis.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I diagnose before I edit: rendered prompt, raw output, finish reason, then a tag — ambiguity, conflict, missing context, bad examples, or weak spec. I change one thing and I re-run the whole set. I do not add a never per incident.
## Worked scenario

Playground works; production fails. You diff traces and find `{{ticket}}` rendered empty because a client sent `Ticket` vs `ticket`. Not a model idea bug. Another pile of failures is prose wrappers — majority tag `weak spec` — so you add a schema, not five nevers.

You diagnose at T=0 on ten failures before editing. You change one thing. The whole set re-runs. A patch-per-bug file from last quarter is consolidated in the same PR.

Editing from memory of the playground text is the original sin. Always the rendered prompt.

## Interview trap

Rendered prompt, raw output, finish reason, then a tag. Majority tag first. One change, whole set. Production vs playground is often a bad substitution or a different version, not a new idea. Diagnose at low T. Five nevers later you will regress. Do not edit from memory of the playground.
## On a real team

A ticket template requires rendered prompt, raw output, finish reason, and a tag before anyone may paste a new never. Weekly the majority tag becomes the only allowed prompt-change theme. Templating bugs (empty variables) have their own dashboard. Low-T reproduction is a checkbox on the incident form. Memory of the playground is not evidence.

## Remember

Diagnosis is a rendered prompt, a raw output, a tag, and one change. Everything else is superstition. Majority tag first. Memory of the playground last.
keyPoints: Read the rendered prompt and raw output, not your memory of them.
Tag misses: ambiguity, conflict, missing context, bad examples, weak spec.
Fix the majority tag first; change one variable at a time.
Reproduce at low temperature so sampling noise is not the story.
Check finish_reason and template substitution before rewriting ideas.
Patch-per-bug prompts regress; consolidate and re-eval.

questions.q: Name steps you take before rewriting a failing prompt.
questions.a: Collect failures, inspect the rendered prompt and raw output, check truncation and templating, tag the cause, reproduce at low temperature, and look for a pattern across cases.

questions.q: After adding five "never do X" rules, new failures appear. Why, and what now?
questions.a: Patches conflict and dilute priority. Consolidate into a coherent prompt, drive from a tagged failure list, and validate on the full set.

questions.q: Most failures are valid prose instead of JSON. Which tag is that?
questions.a: Weak output spec (or missing enforcement). Add a schema / a last-line contract rather than more style rules.

questions.q: The playground works and production fails. First suspicion?
questions.a: Different rendered text: empty variables, different system prompt version, truncated context, or a different model alias. Diff the traces.

questions.q: Why diagnose at low temperature?
questions.a: So you can see systematic instruction failures instead of one unlucky sample. Variance is a later problem.

building-a-small-test-set.explain:
## What it is

A **small test set** is a fixed collection of inputs with expected outputs or a grading rubric. You run every prompt version against it. Start with **20–50** cases if that is all you have; it is far better than none. Source them from real or realistic traffic, then add every production miss you fix. Cover normal, edge (empty, long, multilingual, ambiguous), and known failures.

Without a set you are tasting outputs. Tasting is not iteration.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the difference between a prompt that "felt better in the playground" and a prompt you can revert. Interviewers will ask how you know a change helped. "I have a 40-case set with edges and last week's incidents" is the answer. "I tried a few examples" is not.

## How it works + one small example

Build:

- 10–20 typical tickets from real traffic (redacted).
- 5 edges: empty, huge paste, other language, contradictory, off-topic.
- 5 known production failures, once fixed, stay in the set (regression).
- 3 adversarial / override-style.
- Tags per case (`billing`, `empty`, `override`) so slices are visible.

```
{id, input, gold, tags[], grade: exact|regex|rubric}
```

Hold out a slice you do not tune on if the set grows past ~80. Store it next to the prompt in git. Strip personal data. If you use an LLM judge, validate the judge on a human-labelled subset first.

## Failure modes

1. **Only easy cases.** 98% on 15 toys, 70% in production.

2. **Tuning until the set is memorised.** A 20-case set you edited the prompt toward is no longer a test. Hold out or keep growing with fresh misses.

3. **Wrong gold.** The label in the set is itself an argument. Review gold like code.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I build a small set of normal, edge, and known-failure cases, I keep it next to the prompt, and I add every production miss I fix. Twenty honest cases beat zero. I hold out data when the set grows, and I do not trust a judge I have not checked against humans.
## Worked scenario

You start with 12 typical redacted tickets, 5 edges (empty, huge, other language, contradictory, off-topic), 5 last-week misses, 3 overrides. Each has gold and tags. It lives next to the prompt in git. 98% on 15 toys last quarter had hidden a 70% production. This set is uglier and honest.

A case the team still argues about does not get a silent gold. You resolve the policy first. An LLM judge is checked on a human-labelled subset before you trust it.

Twenty honest cases beat zero. Growing with production misses beats inventing more easy wins.

## Interview trap

Twenty honest cases beat zero. Typical, edge, last week's misses, overrides. Tags, gold you can grade, git next to the prompt, redacted. 98% on 15 toys is a demo reel. Do not silently gold a case the team still argues about. Validate any judge against humans. Grow with production, not with easy inventions.
## On a real team

The set is a required artefact next to the prompt, with a minimum mix of typical/edge/regression/override. PRs that only add easy wins are rejected. Gold disputes block the case until policy is written down. Judges cannot merge without a human-agreement number. Redaction is a CI grep for email-shaped strings.

## Remember

Ugly honest cases next to the prompt beat a beautiful demo reel. Add every production miss. Redact. Hold out when you start to memorise. Gold is policy, so argue it in the PR, not silently.

Say this: I would rather have thirty ugly real cases than a hundred toys. Last week's incident is already a fixture. If we still argue the gold, we do not yet have a task — we have a policy hole.
keyPoints: 20–50 realistic cases beat none; grow with every fixed production miss.
Include empty, long, multilingual, off-topic, and override cases.
Tag cases so you can see which slice moved.
Store the set in git next to the prompt; strip personal data.
Hold out a slice once the set is large enough to overfit.
Validate any LLM judge against a human-labelled subset.

questions.q: What should a starter prompt test set contain?
questions.a: Typical cases from real traffic, edges (empty, long, ambiguous), out-of-scope and adversarial cases, each with gold or a rubric and tags.

questions.q: Your prompt scores 98% on 15 cases but fails in production. Why?
questions.a: The set is too small or too easy, and likely overfit. Add production misses and more diverse edges, and keep a hold-out.

questions.q: A case has no agreed label inside the team. What do you do?
questions.a: Do not silently pick a gold. Resolve the policy, then encode it. Bad gold teaches the prompt the argument, not the task.

questions.q: Where should the test set live?
questions.a: In version control next to the prompt, redacted, so a PR can show score deltas.

questions.q: You want 10 more cases. What is a better source than inventing easy tickets?
questions.a: Last week's production failures (redacted) and a few adversarial overrides. Those are the slices that actually move risk.

comparing-versions-on-the-same-examples.explain:
## What it is

To know if a prompt change helped, run **old and new on the same fixed examples** with the same model and settings, then look at **flipped cases**, not only the average. A version that fixes three and breaks four is not better. A +2% on a 30-case set is one case and is usually noise.

This is controlled comparison. It is the opposite of "I tried it on a new ticket I liked".

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, averages hide regressions on the slice you care about (refunds, empties, a language). Interviewers will ask if you ship a +2 point prompt. The senior answer is: not on 30 cases; I look at flips, I re-run if variance is high, I check cost and latency, I expand the set.

## How it works + one small example

```
# same 40 ids, same model pin, same T
A@7  pass 32/40
B@8  pass 33/40
flips: 14 A→B fix, 13 B→A break, 1 net
```

Record per-tag pass rates. Repeat n times if outputs vary and compare distributions. For subjective quality, pairwise A/B with **hidden identity** and randomised order (see the later note). Log prompt version on the run so the table is reproducible.

Do not change retrieval stubs, tools, or model when you intend to compare prompts. One variable.

## Failure modes

1. **Different examples.** You "tested B on harder tickets". That is two experiments.

2. **Shipping the average.** Net +1 with a new refund-promise break. Read the flips.

3. **One sample at T=0.8.** Noise. Lower T or repeat.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I compare prompt versions on the same cases, same model, same settings, and I read the flipped rows. I do not ship a +2% on thirty tickets. I look at tags, cost, and latency, and I keep the run logged against a prompt id.
## Worked scenario

A@7 is 32/40, B@8 is 33/40 with 14 flips each way. Net +1 is noise and includes a new refund-promise break. You do not ship. You expand the set, lower T, and read the refund tag. A "harder batch" someone used only on B is not a comparison — that is two experiments.

You log the run against prompt versions. Subjective tone, if it matters, is a blind pairwise later, not an unblinded author vote.

Same ids, same model pin, same retrieval stubs. One variable. Flips over averages.

## Interview trap

Same ids, same pin, same stubs. Read flips. +2 on 30 cases is one ticket and is usually noise. A new refund break in the flip list blocks the ship even if the average rose. Testing B on a 'harder batch' is two experiments. Subjective tone needs a blind pairwise, not an author vote.
## On a real team

The eval CLI refuses to compare two prompt ids on different case lists. Flip CSVs attach to the PR. A +2% on n<50 cannot set a ship label without an explicit override and a slice read. Retrieval stubs are pinned in the fixture. Unblinded 'looks nicer' comments are not a review approve.

## Remember

Control the examples or you are not comparing. Flips over averages. A refund break in the flip list vetoes a +1% mean. Same pin, same stubs, logged versions. That is the experiment.

Say this: if the case lists differ, you did not compare prompts, you compared moods. I will show you the flip rows before I show you the mean. A policy-slice break vetoes a green average. Same ids or it is not science.

A comparison without a shared id list is a story. I pin the list, I pin the model, I print the flips, I refuse a 2-point ship on thirty rows. That discipline is the whole note.

Same cases or it is not a comparison. I will keep saying that until the PR changes.
keyPoints: Same inputs, same model, same settings — only the prompt version changes.
Inspect flipped cases; the average can hide a bad break.
A 1–2 case delta on a small set is usually noise.
Repeat runs when sampling variance is material.
Do not change retrieval or model in the same comparison.
Log the run against prompt versions so you can replay it.

questions.q: Why check which individual cases changed, not just the overall score?
questions.a: The average hides regressions. A prompt that fixes three and breaks four is not better. Flip lists show the trade.

questions.q: Version B is +2 points on a 30-case set. Do you ship it?
questions.a: Not on that alone. Two points is one or two cases. Re-run, expand the set, read flips and cost/latency.

questions.q: You tested B on a new batch of "harder" tickets and it lost. What did you fail to control?
questions.a: The example set. Compare A and B on the same ids first; hardness can be a second experiment later.

questions.q: What else belongs in the comparison table besides pass rate?
questions.a: Per-tag rates, flip lists, input/output tokens, p95 latency, and repair/fallback rates if you have them.

questions.q: Subjective tone improved but you did not hide which prompt wrote the reply. What bias is that?
questions.a: You knew which was new and favoured it. Use a blind pairwise (next notes) or a rubric with hidden ids.

reducing-variance-regressions.explain:
## What it is

**Variance** is the same prompt giving different answers across runs. **Regressions** are changes that break something that used to work. You reduce variance with lower temperature, tighter instructions, schemas, targeted examples, and (for critical answers) majority vote. You prevent regressions with a **regression set**, **pinned models**, prompt review, staged rollout, and a rollback.

Temperature 0 is not a bitwise guarantee. Provider aliases move under you. Treat both as facts.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, flaky labels destroy trust even when the average is fine. Silent model updates destroy last quarter's prompt work. Interviewers will ask why a feature died with no prompt change. "Floating alias" plus "no scheduled regression run" is the diagnosis.

## How it works + one small example

Variance levers:

- T and top-p down on parsed paths.
- Schema-constrained outputs.
- Unambiguous instructions; delete conflicting closers.
- Decomposition if one call is mixing skills.
- Self-consistency (n samples, vote) only when the extra cost is worth a critical answer.

Regression levers:

- The golden set on every prompt or model PR.
- Pin `model-2026-xx-xx`, not `model-latest`.
- Review prompt diffs; one intent per version.
- Canary, then rollback to n-1.

```
# weekly job
run golden@main against pinned model
alert if pass_rate drops > threshold or refund-tag breaks
```

## Failure modes

1. **Calling T=0 deterministic in a design doc.** You will be wrong on Tuesday.

2. **No pin.** Marketing changed the alias. Your prompt "regressed".

3. **Voting on everything.** Cost explodes. Reserve it for high-stakes answers.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I cut unnecessary variance with low temperature, schemas, and clear instructions, and I cut regressions with a golden set, pinned models, and rollback. Temperature 0 is not a guarantee. If a feature dies with no prompt change, I look at the model alias first.
## Worked scenario

A feature dies overnight with a clean prompt git. The alias floated. You pin a dated snapshot, add a weekly golden job, and keep n-1. Self-consistency (n=5) is reserved for a high-stakes credit decision, not the tagger.

T=0 is in the design doc as "deterministic". You strike that word. It reduces variance within a snapshot; it does not freeze the vendor.

A canary that breaks the refund tag rolls back before anyone debugs the new copy in production. Safe first, then the notebook.

## Interview trap

Low T, schemas, clear instructions for variance. Golden set, pinned snapshots, n-1 for regressions. T=0 is not a guarantee. A feature that dies with a clean prompt git is an alias until proven otherwise. Vote only on high-stakes answers. Canary rollback before you debug the new copy in prod.
## On a real team

Aliases are banned in the model config schema. A weekly golden job pages on slice drops. n-1 stays warm. Self-consistency is a flag on high-stakes routes only, with a cost annotation. Design docs that say 'T=0 so we are deterministic' fail review. Canary rollback is rehearsed, not invented during the incident.

## Remember

Variance is sampling; regression is change. Low T and schemas for the first, pins and golden jobs for the second. T=0 does not replace either. Rollback is a feature, not an apology.

Say this: I pin the snapshot so last night's alias cannot pretend to be my prompt. I run the golden set on a schedule. I keep n-1 warm. Variance I treat with T and schemas; regressions I treat with process. T=0 is not a freeze spell.
keyPoints: Lower T, clearer instructions, and schemas reduce variance.
Majority vote is for critical answers, not for every call.
Run a regression set on every prompt or model change.
Pin model snapshots; floating aliases are silent prompt changes.
Temperature 0 is not bitwise deterministic.
Keep n-1 ready; staged rollout beats a Friday overwrite.

questions.q: List ways to reduce output variance.
questions.a: Lower temperature and top-p, clearer instructions, structured outputs, targeted examples, decomposition, optional seeds, and self-consistency voting for critical answers.

questions.q: Last week's feature died with no prompt change. What happened and what prevents repeats?
questions.a: Likely a provider update under a floating alias, or changed upstream data. Pin versions, run the regression set on a schedule, and monitor slice metrics.

questions.q: Should every request use self-consistency (n=5 vote)?
questions.a: No. It multiplies cost and latency. Use it where a wrong answer is expensive and a single sample is noisy.

questions.q: Why is T=0 not enough to skip a regression set after a model pin change?
questions.a: A new snapshot can change the mode you were sampling. T=0 only reduces variance within a snapshot.

questions.q: A canary shows the refund tag breaking. What do you do before debugging the new copy?
questions.a: Roll back to n-1 so production is safe, then debug the new version offline on the golden set.

failure-taxonomy-for-prompts.explain:
## What it is

A **failure taxonomy for prompts** is a small set of tags you put on every miss: **ambiguity**, **conflict**, **missing context**, **bad examples**, **weak output spec** (plus, if you want, knowledge and tool-use). The tag chooses the fix. Without tags you will add examples to a missing-context problem and add rules to a schema problem.

This is the same list you use while diagnosing, written down so a team shares it.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a weekly histogram of tags tells you where to spend time. If 60% is weak spec, you buy structured output, not more shots. Interviewers will ask "how do you categorise prompt failures?" Reciting this list, and naming the fix per tag, is a complete answer.

## How it works + one small example

| Tag | Symptom | First fix |
| ambiguity | two readings of a rule | one sentence, one example of the boundary |
| conflict | two rules fight | delete or state precedence |
| missing context | fact not in the prompt | retrieve or inject state |
| bad examples | shots disagree or imbalance | fix the fixtures |
| weak spec | shape/enum drift | schema + last-line contract |

```
# week 12 histogram
weak spec 14
missing   6
conflict  3
```

You can add `injection` and `truncation` as operational tags so they do not pollute the prompt-idea histogram. Keep the set small or people will invent a new tag per ticket.

## Failure modes

1. **Too many tags.** A taxonomy nobody uses. Five is enough.

2. **Tag as blame.** "Bad model" is not a tag that changes your next edit.

3. **Fixing the untagged singleton first.** Work the pile.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I tag misses as ambiguity, conflict, missing context, bad examples, or weak output spec, and the tag picks the fix. A histogram of those tags is how I decide whether to add examples, retrieve, or turn on a schema.
## Worked scenario

Week 12 histogram: weak spec 14, missing context 6, conflict 3. You buy a schema, then retrieval, then you delete a fighting closer. You do not add examples to the missing-context pile. "Bad model" is not a tag on the board.

Operational tags (`truncation`, `injection`) sit to the side so they do not pollute the idea histogram. Five prompt tags is enough; a 20-tag scheme will not be used.

The taxonomy is how a team shares diagnosis. Write the fix next to each tag on the wiki once, then stop re-litigating.

## Interview trap

Ambiguity, conflict, missing context, bad examples, weak spec. The tag picks the fix. A weekly histogram tells you whether to buy a schema or retrieval. 'Bad model' is not a tag. Keep it to five plus a couple of operational labels or nobody will use it. Work the pile, not the singleton.
## On a real team

The five tags are a dropdown on the incident form. A monthly histogram goes to the team meeting and picks the next prompt investment. 'Bad model' is not in the dropdown. Operational tags sit beside it. New tags need a one-page fix mapping or they are rejected. Shared language is the point of the taxonomy.

## Remember

Five tags, five first fixes, one histogram. If you cannot pick a tag you do not yet know what to edit. 'Bad model' is not on the list because it does not change tonight's diff.

Say this: tell me which of the five tags this miss is, and I will tell you tonight's edit. No tag, no edit. The histogram picks the quarter's work. That is how a team stops relitigating every incident from zero.

Put the five tags on the wall. The next edit must name one. That is how diagnosis becomes a habit instead of a debate.
keyPoints: Five useful tags: ambiguity, conflict, missing context, bad examples, weak spec.
The tag chooses the fix; do not add shots to a retrieval problem.
Keep a weekly histogram; work the majority pile first.
Operational issues (truncation, injection) get their own tags.
"Bad model" is not a prompt-failure tag.
A small shared taxonomy beats a unique essay per incident.

questions.q: Name a practical failure taxonomy for prompts.
questions.a: Ambiguity, conflict, missing context, bad examples, and weak output spec. Each maps to a different first fix.

questions.q: 60% of misses are prose wrappers around the right label. Which tag and fix?
questions.a: Weak output spec. Add a schema and a last-line contract rather than more label definitions.

questions.q: You added five examples and the miss was that the policy doc was never retrieved. Which tag did you ignore?
questions.a: Missing context. Examples cannot supply a document that was not in the prompt.

questions.q: Two sentences in the system prompt disagree on length. Which tag?
questions.a: Conflict. Delete one or state precedence; do not add a third adjective.

questions.q: Why keep the taxonomy small?
questions.a: People will not apply a 20-tag scheme, and you cannot histogram it. Five tags plus a couple of operational ones is enough to choose a fix.

golden-set-design.explain:
## What it is

A **golden set** is a curated eval that is more intentional than "some tickets we had". It includes **easy**, **borderline**, **adversarial**, and **regression** cases, each with an **expected shape** (exact object, regex, or rubric). Easy cases guard against catastrophic breaks. Borderline cases are where prompt work happens. Adversarial cases (overrides, empty, prompt-in-data) guard abuse. Regression cases are yesterday's bugs, kept forever.

Design the set the way you design a test suite, not a demo reel.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a golden set is what lets you change a system prompt on a Friday. Interviewers will ask what is in it. If you only say "real tickets", you missed edges and attacks. If you only say "jailbreaks", you missed the easy path that a rewrite can smash.

## How it works + one small example

Aim for a mix, not a pile of one type:

```
easy        30%   obvious billing / obvious bug
borderline  30%   sarcasm, two-intent, mixed
adversarial 20%   empty, override, leaked-instruction docs
regression  20%   every fixed production miss
```

Each row has gold **shape** (`label`, `status`) and, where needed, a semantic note. Version the set (`golden@5`). When policy changes (what "urgent" means), update gold in the same PR as the prompt. Redact. If the set becomes famous inside the team, add a hold-out so you are not overfitting to folklore cases.

## Failure modes

1. **Demo reel.** Only cases the current prompt already wins. Useless.

2. **Stale gold after a policy change.** The set now punishes the correct new behaviour.

3. **No expected shape.** A paragraph gold you cannot grade automatically, and nobody grades it by hand either.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A golden set mixes easy, borderline, adversarial, and regression cases with an expected shape on each row. I version it, I update gold when policy changes, and I keep last week's bugs in it so they cannot return silently.
## Worked scenario

You rebuild the set as 30% easy, 30% borderline, 20% adversarial, 20% regression. Last week's bugs stay forever. Policy changes (sarcasm is now billing) update gold in the same PR as the prompt. A 40-case demo reel that already scores 100% is discarded as folklore.

Each row has an expected shape you can grade. A prose note nobody scores is decoration. Real emails are rewritten as fictional analogues.

Version the set `golden@5`. When it becomes famous, add a hold-out so you are not overfitting to campfire stories.

## Interview trap

Easy, borderline, adversarial, regression, each with a shape. Update gold in the same PR as a policy change. Keep fixed bugs forever. A 100% demo reel cannot detect a regression. Version the set. Redact. Add a hold-out when the set becomes folklore. Prose gold nobody scores is decoration.
## On a real team

golden@N lives in git. Policy PRs that change a definition must touch gold in the same change. A job fails if easy-only coverage exceeds a threshold. Folklore cases get a hold-out twin. Expected shape is a schema, not a comment. When someone wants a 'showcase set' for demos, it is a different file that cannot gate ships.

## Remember

Easy guards the floor, borderline is where you work, adversarial guards abuse, regression keeps last week's bugs dead. Shape on every row. Policy and gold move together. Demos live elsewhere.

Say this: the set is a test suite, not a highlight reel. Easy, borderline, attack, and last week's bugs, each with a shape. When policy moves, gold moves in the same PR. Demos do not gate ships.
keyPoints: Mix easy, borderline, adversarial, and regression rows.
Every row has an expected shape you can grade.
Keep fixed production bugs as regression cases forever.
Version the set and update gold in the same PR as a policy change.
Avoid a demo reel of cases you already pass.
Redact personal data; add a hold-out if the set becomes folklore.

questions.q: What four kinds of cases belong in a golden set?
questions.a: Easy, borderline, adversarial (empty/override), and regression (fixed production misses), each with an expected shape.

questions.q: Policy changed: sarcasm about charges is now billing, not other. What do you update together?
questions.a: The prompt (or label definition) and the golden rows for those tickets, in one PR, so the set does not punish the new rule.

questions.q: Your golden set is 40 tickets the current prompt already scores 100% on. What is wrong?
questions.a: It is a demo reel. Add borderline, adversarial, and recent failures or you cannot detect a regression that matters.

questions.q: Why keep an expected shape, not only a prose note?
questions.a: So you can grade automatically (exact label, schema, sentinel). A prose note nobody scores is decoration.

questions.q: A golden case still contains a real email address. What do you do?
questions.a: Redact or rewrite as a fictional analogue that keeps the judgement. Eval sets are logged and copied.

blind-comparison-and-inter-rater.explain:
## What it is

**Blind comparison** means the human (or judge model) who scores quality **does not see** which prompt produced the output. **Inter-rater** means two people score the same items so you can see if your rubric is real. Together they stop you from shipping the version you already liked.

Pairwise A vs B with randomised order is the usual design. A score of 4.6 vs 4.4 from one person who knew B was "the new one" is not evidence.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, prompt authors are biased. Blind pairwise is how you evaluate tone, helpfulness, and other soft traits that exact match cannot see. Interviewers will ask how you evaluate subjective quality. If you do not mention blinding and a second rater (or a judge validated against humans), you are describing taste.

## How it works + one small example

```
item 19
  left  = output of prompt B   # hidden
  right = output of prompt A
  rater picks left|right|tie using a 4-line rubric
```

Randomise left/right. Hide ids. Collect 2 raters on a subset; if they disagree a lot, the rubric is vague — fix the rubric before you trust the winner. If you use an LLM judge, run it against those human pairs first and publish the agreement. Do not let the judge see the prompt text.

For hard policy traits (did it refund?), prefer exact checks over raters. Blind pairwise is for the leftover subjective column.

## Failure modes

1. **Author as sole rater, unblinded.** You will pick your child.

2. **Vague rubric.** "Which is better?" Raters split. Specify audience and three yes/no questions.

3. **Judge sees the prompt.** It will prefer the longer constitution.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

When humans score quality I hide which prompt produced the output, I randomise order, and I measure agreement between raters. If they disagree, I fix the rubric. I do not use unblinded taste as a ship gate.
## Worked scenario

The prompt author preferred B in an unblinded read. You run pairwise with hidden ids, randomised left/right, and a 4-line rubric. Two raters disagree on half. You fix the rubric (audience + three yes/no) before you trust a winner. An LLM judge is accepted only after it matches those pairs, and it never sees the prompt text.

Refund-promise detection stays a regex. Raters are for leftover tone, not for policy.

Unblinded taste is not a ship gate. Agreement is part of the metric.

## Interview trap

Hide ids, randomise order, short rubric. If two raters split, fix the rubric before you trust a winner. Validate an LLM judge on those pairs and never let it see the prompt. Policy traits (refunds) are exact checks, not pairwise taste. Unblinded author preference is not a ship gate.
## On a real team

The rating UI hides ids and randomises order by construction. A second rater is required on a sample before a subjective ship. Judge-prompt versions are logged. Policy checks never go through this UI. If agreement is low, the rubric PR comes first. Author self-rates are dropped from the official table.

## Remember

If the rater knows which prompt is new, you measured attachment. Hide ids, randomise, agree on a rubric, then maybe a judge. Policy stays exact. Taste is not a gate until it is blind.

Say this: I will not let the author of B score B with the lights on. Hide the id, flip the order, measure agreement, then maybe trust a judge. Refunds are a regex. Taste waits its turn.

Lights off, order shuffled, two raters, rubric first. Anything less is the author grading their homework. I will say that in the interview.
keyPoints: Hide prompt identity; randomise A/B order.
Use a short rubric, not "which is better?".
Measure inter-rater agreement; disagreement means a bad rubric.
Validate an LLM judge against human pairs before trusting it.
Do not let a judge see the prompt text.
Prefer exact checks for policy traits; pairwise is for leftover subjective quality.

questions.q: What does a blind comparison hide?
questions.a: Which prompt (or model) produced each output, so the rater cannot favour the new one. Order is randomised as well.

questions.q: Two raters disagree on half the pairs. What do you fix first?
questions.a: The rubric. Write audience and three concrete yes/no questions, then re-rate a subset. Do not average a coin flip.

questions.q: How do you use an LLM judge responsibly here?
questions.a: Blind it to prompt identity, run it on items humans already labelled, and only trust it if agreement is acceptable. Recheck when you change the judge prompt.

questions.q: Should refund-promise detection be a pairwise human task?
questions.a: No. That is an exact or regex check. Save raters for tone and helpfulness.

questions.q: Why randomise left/right even if ids are hidden?
questions.a: People (and some judges) have position bias and prefer the first or second essay. Randomisation averages that out.

pinning-model-versions.explain:
## What it is

**Pinning model versions** means you call a **snapshot** (`gpt-x-2026-mm-dd`, a dated Claude snapshot, a Gemini version id) while you iterate a prompt, so **model drift is not confused with prompt drift**. Floating aliases (`latest`, `current`, a marketing name) can change weights under you. Your golden set then moves and you will "debug the prompt" for a week.

Pin in config. Log the resolved id. When you intend to upgrade the model, that is a separate experiment: same prompt, new pin, same set.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the silent-outage class. Interviewers will ask why quality fell overnight. "Alias moved" is a mature answer. "The model got worse" is not a plan. Say you pin, you re-run the golden set on a schedule against the pin, and you upgrade on purpose.

## How it works + one small example

```
# config
model: claude-…-2026-05-01
prompt: sys-support@12
```

Practices:

- No `latest` in production.
- Resolve and log the id the API actually used if the provider returns it.
- A weekly job: golden set × current pin; alert on drops.
- Upgrade PR: new pin, same prompt, table of deltas; then a second PR if the prompt must adapt.
- Keep the old pin available until the new one passes canary.

Providers differ in how they name snapshots. Read current docs. The idea is portable.

## Failure modes

1. **Alias in prod, pin in staging.** You tested nothing.

2. **Changing pin and prompt together.** You cannot attribute.

3. **No scheduled re-run.** Even pins can be retired; you want a warning, not a customer.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I freeze the model snapshot while I iterate the prompt so I do not confuse model drift with prompt drift. Upgrades are a separate experiment on the same golden set. I do not run `latest` in production.
## Worked scenario

Staging pinned; production used `latest`. Tuesday's quality drop was an alias move. You pin prod too, log the resolved id, and split upgrades into two PRs: pin-only with a golden table, then prompt adapt if needed. The old pin stays for rollback.

Changing pin and prompt together last quarter made a "win" you still cannot explain. One variable.

A weekly job against the current pin is how you learn a snapshot was retired before customers do.

## Interview trap

Snapshot while you iterate the prompt. Upgrade is a separate PR: same prompt, new pin, same set, then adapt if needed. `latest` in prod with a pin in staging tests nothing. Log the resolved id. Weekly golden against the pin. Never change pin and prompt together if you want attribution.
## On a real team

Config schema rejects latest/current. Upgrade tickets are pin-only first. Staging and prod share the same pin field. Resolved ids are logged and compared to config. A calendar reminder exists for vendor retirement dates. Combined pin+prompt PRs are split in review with a checklist item.

## Remember

A floating alias is a silent prompt change. Pin, log the resolved id, upgrade on purpose, keep n-1. Staging and prod must tell the same story or you tested a ghost.

Say this: latest is not an environment, it is a surprise. I pin, I log what actually served, I upgrade as its own experiment, I keep the old pin. Staging that lies about prod is how Tuesday happens.

The snapshot is part of the prompt. Change it on purpose or do not change it. latest is how quality falls while git stays clean. I pin both sides of the experiment.

Pin the snapshot. Upgrade on purpose. That is the whole pin story.
keyPoints: Pin a dated snapshot while iterating prompts.
Treat a model upgrade as its own experiment: same prompt, new pin, same set.
Do not use latest/current aliases in production.
Log the resolved model id on every trace.
Schedule a golden-set run so retirement or silent change is visible.
Never change pin and prompt in the same PR if you want attribution.

questions.q: Why pin a model snapshot while you iterate a prompt?
questions.a: So a weight change cannot be mistaken for a prompt regression. You want one variable per experiment.

questions.q: Quality dropped overnight, prompt git is clean. What do you check first?
questions.a: Whether the serving alias moved, and what model id the traces actually logged. Re-run the golden set on the last known pin.

questions.q: How do you upgrade a model safely?
questions.a: A PR that only changes the pin, golden-set table, canary, then adapt the prompt in a second PR if needed. Keep the old pin for rollback.

questions.q: Staging pins a snapshot; production uses latest. What is the hole?
questions.a: You never tested what production will run tomorrow. Prod must pin too.

questions.q: What belongs in the trace next to prompt_version?
questions.a: The resolved model id (and key params such as temperature). Together they name the generator.

logging-traces-for-debug.explain:
## What it is

A **debug trace** is the minimum record that lets you **replay** a failure: **prompt id/version**, **model**, **input hash** (or redacted input), **raw output**, finish reason, token counts, schema-pass, and tool args your code accepted. Without this you are guessing from a screenshot of the UI.

Logging is not "dump the world". Personal text has rules: hash when you can, redact when you must, restrict who can see raw payloads. Never log secrets that were not supposed to be in the prompt anyway.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, "it said something weird" is not a ticket you can work. A trace is. Interviewers will ask what you store. If you say "the whole prompt including the customer's card number" you fail privacy. If you say "nothing, privacy" you fail operability. The balance is the note.

## How it works + one small example

```
{
  "prompt_id": "sys-support",
  "prompt_version": 12,
  "model": "…-2026-05-01",
  "input_hash": "sha256:…",
  "example_ids": ["ex_88"],
  "raw_output": "…",
  "finish": "stop",
  "usage": {"in": 900, "out": 40, "cached": 700},
  "schema_ok": true
}
```

Keep raw output for a retention window. Store the rendered prompt only if policy allows, else store hashes and the variable ids. For dynamic few-shot, store example ids. For tools, store the **accepted** arguments, not only the model's proposal.

Make a replay command: given a trace id, rebuild the request from versioned artefacts and the stored (or re-fetched) input.

## Failure modes

1. **UI-only evidence.** You cannot see the assembled prompt.

2. **PII museum.** You logged everything forever with broad access.

3. **No hash.** You cannot even tell two "same" tickets apart.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I store prompt version, model, an input hash, and the raw output so a failure is replayable. I redact or restrict personal text, I log accepted tool args, and I can rebuild the request from versioned artefacts. A screenshot of the chat is not a trace.
## Worked scenario

Tickets arrive as "the bot was weird" plus a screenshot. You require a trace id. From it you load prompt@12, the pinned model, input hash, raw output, finish, usage (including cached tokens), schema_ok, and example_ids. You can replay. Bodies are redacted and access-restricted; you do not run a PII museum.

Dynamic few-shot without example ids is not replayable. Child repair calls without stamps are invisible cost.

A screenshot is not a trace. The minimum record is what makes the next incident a replay instead of a guess.

## Interview trap

prompt_version, model, input hash, raw output, finish, usage, schema_ok, example_ids, accepted tool args. Replay from artefacts. Screenshots are not traces. Restrict PII; do not run a museum. Stamp child calls. Cached-token fields are how you diagnose a 0% hit rate. Operability and privacy are both required.
## On a real team

Trace id is the first question in the support macro. Access to raw bodies is role-gated and time-bounded. Child spans are required by the tracing library. Cached tokens are a first-class field. A quarterly privacy review asks what you still store. 'We have screenshots' is not a close reason on an incident.

## Remember

Replay or it did not happen. Version, model, hash, raw output, children, cache counts. Restrict bodies. A screenshot is a courtesy, not a record. Privacy and operability are the same ticket.

Say this: give me the trace id or we are guessing. I can rebuild the request from versions and a hash. Children are stamped. Bodies are gated. Screenshots are optional. That is a debug culture, not a folder of PNGs.
keyPoints: Minimum replay record: prompt version, model, input hash, raw output.
Log finish reason, usage (including cached tokens), and schema_ok.
Redact or restrict PII; hash when you do not need the raw input.
Store accepted tool arguments and dynamic example ids.
A replay path from trace id back to versioned artefacts is the point.
Do not treat a UI screenshot as sufficient debug evidence.

questions.q: What four fields make a failure replayable?
questions.a: Prompt id/version, model, a reference to the input (hash or redacted body), and the raw output. Finish reason and usage are the usual extras.

questions.q: A ticket is "the bot was weird" with a screenshot. What do you ask for?
questions.a: The trace id. From it you should load prompt version, model, rendered or hashed input, and raw output. A screenshot is not enough.

questions.q: You logged full ticket bodies in a world-readable bucket. What did you get wrong?
questions.a: Retention and access. Hash or redact, restrict viewers, and never store secrets. Operability does not require a PII museum.

questions.q: Why log cached-token counts on the trace?
questions.a: So a 0% hit rate can be diagnosed as a layout bug, and so cost explanations are not guesses.

questions.q: Dynamic few-shot traces omit example ids. What can you not do?
questions.a: Replay the demonstrations that actually sat in the prompt, so you cannot tell if retrieval caused the miss.

interview.explain:
## What it is

**Interview: how you iterate a prompt** is a four-beat story: **measure** on a fixed set, **change one thing**, **re-run the same set**, **keep or revert**. That is the whole reliability module in one breath. You may mention tags, blindness, pins, and traces as supporting gear. You may not mention "I tweak until it feels right".

This is the Level 3 process question. Content questions (anatomy, few-shot) sit beside it. Process is what makes those edits honest.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers are listening for scientific control. One variable, same examples, a written keep/revert rule, a version id. On the job this is also how you stop a room of stakeholders from parallel-editing a dashboard. The story you tell in the interview is the process you should already be running.

## How it works + one small example

Speak this sequence:

1. **Measure.** Golden set (easy/borderline/adversarial/regression), pinned model, logged prompt@n. Baseline numbers including cost.
2. **Change one thing.** One tag's fix: spec, example, retrieval, or a deleted conflict — not four at once.
3. **Re-run the same ids.** Table of flips, tags, tokens, p95. Blind pairwise if the trait is subjective.
4. **Keep or revert.** Keep only if the bar moves without a policy-slice break. Mint `prompt@n+1`. Roll back if canary fails.

Offer a 30-case starter if they ask how small is too small: good enough to start, not enough to ship a 2-point delta. Mention you will not confuse a model alias move with this loop.

## Failure modes

1. **Feeling-driven iteration.** No set, no revert rule.

2. **Kitchen-sink diffs.** You cannot name what worked.

3. **No production pin/log.** The interview process dies on first contact with prod.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I measure on a fixed set, I change one thing, I re-run the same cases, and I keep or revert. I pin the model, I log the prompt version, and I read flips not vibes. That is how a prompt change earns its keep.
## Worked scenario

You tell the four beats: measure, change one thing, re-run the same ids, keep or revert. A stakeholder wants five "small" edits in one PR; you split them. You will not keep a change because two playground answers looked nicer. You pin the model and log prompt_version so the loop survives production.

You revert even if the average rose, when the refund slice broke. A 2-point move on 30 cases is not a ship gate. Canary plus rollback is part of "keep".

Feeling-driven iteration is the anti-story. Scientific control is the story.

## Interview trap

Measure, change one thing, re-run the same ids, keep or revert. Split kitchen-sink PRs. Do not keep a change because two playground answers looked nicer. Pin and log so the loop survives prod. Revert an average win that broke a policy slice. A 2-point move on 30 cases is not a gate. Canary is part of keep.
## On a real team

The four beats are in the contributing guide. Prompt PRs that change more than one tagged thing are split. Keep/revert is a required PR section with flips attached. Canary is on the merge checklist. People who 'just tweaked it until it felt right' do not get to publish to prod, including staff engineers.

## Remember

Four beats, one variable, same ids, keep or revert. That sentence is the module. Everything else — tags, blinds, pins, traces — is gear that makes those beats honest in production.

Say this: measure, change one thing, re-run the same set, keep or revert. I will split your five-edit PR. I will not ship a vibe. Canary is part of keep. That is how I iterate a prompt, on a whiteboard and on a Friday.
keyPoints: Iterate: measure, change one thing, re-run the same set, keep or revert.
One tagged fix per version; kitchen-sink diffs cannot be attributed.
Read flips, tags, and cost — not a playground feeling.
Pin the model and log prompt_version so the loop survives production.
A 2-point move on 30 cases is not a ship gate.
Canary plus rollback is part of "keep", not a later luxury.

questions.q: Describe how you iterate a prompt, in four beats.
questions.a: Measure on a fixed golden set, change one thing aimed at a tagged miss, re-run the same ids, and keep or revert based on flips and the quality bar.

questions.q: A stakeholder wants five prompt edits in one PR because they are "all small". What do you do?
questions.a: Split them. One variable per version so the re-run can attribute a win or a break.

questions.q: You kept a change because two playground answers "looked nicer". What was missing?
questions.a: The same-set re-run, a flip list, and (for tone) a blind pairwise. Looking nicer is not a keep rule.

questions.q: What do you pin and log so this loop works in production?
questions.a: Model snapshot and prompt_version (plus enough trace fields to replay). Otherwise you cannot re-run "the same" anything.

questions.q: When do you revert even if the average went up?
questions.a: When a policy slice broke (refunds, empty, override) or cost/latency blew the budget. Averages are not the keep rule by themselves.

versioning-prompts-like-code.explain:
## What it is

**Versioning prompts like code** means the text that steers the model lives in **git or a registry**, changes go through **review**, each published text has an **id**, and every production result is **joined to that id plus the model**. A prompt is application logic. A string literal in three handlers is unreviewed logic.

This includes system prompts, task templates, tool preambles, and judge prompts. If it changes behaviour, it gets a version.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview
